text:
I think one of the biggest misconceptions about trading is that markets are mainly about candles, patterns, support, resistance and predicting where price goes next.

A candle is just the final representation of thousands of orders, participants, models, algorithms, liquidity conditions and probabilities interacting at the same time.

Underneath the chart you have market makers managing inventory, HFT firms competing for queue priority, execution algos breaking down institutional orders, dealers hedging exposure, stat-arb models exploiting small mispricings and quant funds constantly updating probabilities as new information enters the system.

At its core, trading is basically an attempt to estimate something close to:

P(Rₜ₊₁ | Xₜ)

The distribution of future returns given the information available right now.

The problem is that this distribution is not stationary. Volatility changes, correlations change, liquidity changes, participants change and regimes change. Variables that had predictive power for months can slowly lose it.

That is where alpha decay comes in.

Imagine a strategy with a 55% win rate, an average win of 1.5R and an average loss of 1R.

Its expectancy is +0.375R per trade.

Now reduce the average winner from 1.5R to 0.9R because of more competition, worse execution, slippage or a regime shift.

The win rate is still 55%, but expectancy is now almost zero.

Add spread, fees and market impact and the strategy can already be negative.

This is also why win rate alone tells you almost nothing. A strategy can win 70% of the time and still lose money, while one with a 35% win rate can have a strong edge if its winners are large enough and the return distribution has positive skew.

What matters is the distribution behind those trades: expectancy, variance, skew, kurtosis, tail risk, drawdown, serial correlation and risk of ruin.

Then you have an even harder question: is the edge actually real?

If you test enough indicators, parameters, stops and filters, eventually something will look incredible purely by chance.

That is multiple testing and overfitting.

A perfect backtest does not necessarily mean you discovered an inefficiency. You may have simply selected the best-looking noise out of hundreds of hypotheses.

This is why a high Sharpe ratio by itself means very little.

You need sample size, out-of-sample testing, walk-forward validation, parameter stability and Monte Carlo simulations. You also need to account for selection bias with measures like the Deflated Sharpe Ratio.

Regime dependency makes it even harder.

A strategy could have a Sharpe of 2.5 during high-volatility trends, 0.5 during normal conditions and -1.5 during low-vol chop.

Look only at the full backtest and it might look like a universal edge, when in reality it is just a hidden bet on a specific market regime.

Then there is capacity.

An edge that works with $100k might stop working with $100M because eventually your own size becomes part of the market impact you are trying to exploit.

Fills get worse, execution deteriorates and an inefficiency that looked huge on paper becomes much harder to monetize.

This is why trading is far more complex than what social media makes it look like.

You are trying to find a small statistical asymmetry inside a competitive, adaptive and non-stationary system, prove it is not noise, execute it after real-world frictions and then hope it survives as more capital discovers the same thing.

Even real alpha does not last forever.

The more exploitable an inefficiency becomes, the more capital flows into it and the faster those excess returns get arbitraged away.

Finding a setup that “worked” is easy.

Proving that a positive expectation is real, understanding why it exists, knowing when it starts decaying and surviving long enough for the statistics to actually matter is the real game.

DHH is fundamentally right about Rust. For context, Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification (carcinization, technically 🦀) for a while.

One of the first projects we migrated was Turborepo, from Go to Rust¹. The migration completed, but the RoI was actually quite controversial internally.

While Rust was in our eyes better for low-level OS access, something crucial for a build system like Turbo, the human migration costs were very sustantive.

Go is very fast. It's beautifully designed. It's easy to iterate on. We were very conflicted about the migration, because it was *humans* writing the code, *even if we knew Rust was a better choice*.

The calculus has now changed. What's "best for humans" is no longer necessarily "best for business". 

FWIW, it's also quite unlikely that Rust is the end-all-be-all toolchain. I'm quite certain there's greener pasture ahead, because Rust itself was designed before the 'supersonic tsunami' of agents hit.

¹ https​://vercel.com/blog/how-turborepo-is-porting-from-go-to-rust

text:
Dear followers,

I need your help.

This Tuesday I am launching my second book, How To Live An Extraordinary Life Volume 2. Usually a book launch has tons of support from big publishers, expensive marketing campaigns, mainstream media interviews, and thousands of shelves in bookstores across the country.

I’m doing this launch independently because I believe the power of community trumps any other approach.

So here is my big ask: If I have ever provided you any value, please consider buying a book. If I helped you make money, consider grabbing a copy. If I gave you a new idea to think about, buy a book. And if you were ever entertained by the podcast, my tweets, or this letter, order a few copies and then tell your friends to do the same.

Order here: https://t.co/KW3fShIMZf

We are hosting a book launch event on Thursday night at City Winery in Manhattan. My wife, @polinapompliano, will be interviewing me on stage. I am terrified of what insane questions she will ask me or what stories she will make me recount, but there is no going back now that I have committed to the event.

It will be unlike any event we have done before. You can get a ticket to Thursday’s event here: https://t.co/FeYGHeVEMa 

I sent an early copy to a few friends and they seemed to like it.

- @theRealKiyosaki, Author of NYT bestseller “Rich Dad Poor Dad” said: “It’s filled with wisdom all of us need…a must-read for every parent to give their child.”

- @Scaramucci, financier and former White House Communications Director, said: “fifty ideas that can change your life, written by one of the sharpest minds in finance and one of the best fathers I know.”

I spent a year writing about 50 life-changing ideas that had a significant impact on me. These lessons span across my personal, professional, and financial life, including:

- The two types of men in the morning
- Why it is better to be busy than bored
- How to be the 60% spouse
- What the Production Principle is
- How I define success now
- The importance of “F**k you focus”
- Why more people die on the way down from Mount Everest
- Why you must avoid Chauffeur Knowledge
- What to learn when dissent is outlawed
- The difference between ordinary and extraordinary
- How the devil doesn’t tempt you with spinach

I am not measuring success of this book by the number of books we sell. I want the ideas to speak for themselves. The true test of a book’s quality is whether it can spread through word of mouth with no marketing gimmicks. I don’t care about book club stickers or bestseller lists. I just want each of you to say, “This brought me immense value.”

Order here: https://t.co/KW3fShIMZf 

Thank you in advance for the support. It means a lot to me. I look forward to continuing to learn alongside you in the coming years.

author: ika_xbt
quoted_text:
Seeing a lot of takes on Abstract today. Mine is simple:

Liquidity precedes culture.

Monad, Berachain, Abstract, and MegaETH all tried to build culture before launch, or on the promise of future liquidity. What you get is artificial culture, propped up by expectations.

→ Ethereum NFT communities wouldn't have thrived without the DeFi summer that came before them
→ Solana memecoins wouldn't have thrived without the airdrop season that came before them

The money came first. The culture grew on top of it.

That's why, on a mid-to-long-term horizon, I think arbitrum has a real shot. The liquidity is already there.

What's missing are a few pieces to turn it into culture. I'd say:
→ A liquidity injection, like the VAR TGE
→ Growing chain revenue, so they can do buybacks (even minor ones) as a sign of alignment
→ A fully unlocked supply, for the narrative
→ After strengthening their core TradFi offering, another bet from the DAO into the consumer segment (following the failed gaming attempt).

text:
HuggingFace just closed a major gap in harness engineering!

(the ultimate guide to multi-harness RL)

the same open-weight model can perform well inside one harness, then lose accuracy or produce invalid tool calls when moved to another.

this happens because training inside one interface can teach the model its specific tool names, output formats, context structure, and control flow. the model learns how to operate the harness, not just how to solve the task.

Hugging Face researchers tested a more portable approach called multi-harness reinforcement learning. instead of training a model through one agent interface, they trained it through Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Mini-SWE-Agent.

to make that possible, they connected three open systems.

→ 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗘𝗻𝘃 provides a standard interface between agent harnesses, reinforcement learning environments, and trainers. its capture proxy sits between the harness and model server, recording the exact tokens and generation probabilities needed for training.

→ 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗼𝗿 runs agents against containerized tasks. it keeps the task, harness, and sandbox independent, allowing the same task to be attempted through different harnesses without rebuilding the environment.

→ 𝗧𝗥𝗟 is Hugging Face’s open-source library for post-training language models. it uses the trajectories captured by 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗘𝗻𝘃 to update the model through reinforcement learning.

the real breakthrough is where the training data gets captured.

each harness keeps its native tools, prompts, context management, retries, and execution loop. the researchers do not recreate those behaviors inside the trainer. 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗘𝗻𝘃 observes the model calls passing through each real harness and converts them into usable training sequences.

the team trained 𝗟𝗙𝗠𝟮.𝟱-𝟮.𝟲𝗕 across all four harnesses. the share of held-out tasks solved on the first attempt increased from 42.2% to 54.2%, with gains under every harness.

the trained model also used 31% fewer tool calls on tasks that both it and the base model solved.

training only in OpenCode improved the model too, but most of that gain stayed concentrated in OpenCode. multi-harness training spread the improvement across interfaces.

the experiment used one task family, one training seed, and unequal data exposure, so the results are not a universal ranking. even with those limitations, the mechanism matters.

open-source models cannot assume one deployment interface. if they need to work across harnesses, that portability must become part of training.

Read the full guide here: https://t.co/BFJfbFmI3J

if you want to understand harness engineering and what an agent harness actually includes, i wrote a full breakdown to help you get started. the article is quoted below.

text:
Hot take: faster chip design won’t necessarily overwhelm fabs. My prediction is that poor first-pass silicon success will be the bigger bottleneck in scaling custom silicon.

The usual concern is more designs = more tapeouts = overwhelmed fabs. But I think that misses a key variable: how often each design has to come back.

In Siemens’ 2026 study, only 5% of IC/ASIC respondents reported first-silicon success. As custom silicon becomes more ubiquitous, my bet is that repeat spins become a much bigger source of capacity pressure. 

But if the tools making design faster also improve first-pass success, we can reduce repeat fabrication per successful design. I expect that to absorb a meaningful share of the additional prototyping demand. Faster design and better first-pass success need to happen together.

Also not every custom chip needs 2nm TSMC tapeout lol. Mature nodes already serve applications from power management to connectivity. For instance, GlobalFoundries 12LP is already great for aerospace. I expect faster design cycles to unlock more applications on those processes, spreading opportunity across more foundries. TSMC stays top dog, but they won’t have the 72% market share that they have now and others will get a bigger piece of the pie. 

IMO, scaling custom silicon is as much about avoiding repeat spins as adding fab capacity.

This requires an end to end disruption in the EDA space - we can’t just keep building new interfaces that call legacy EDA engines (*cough* GPT Synopsys *cough) The goal is to unlock more new designs and eliminate repeat builds. (The fabs may not want this bc $$$ but 🤷‍♂️)

text:
Andrej Karpathy built an agent that runs AI research autonomously. The whole setup is just 3 files

It's called autoresearch. You give Claude or Codex a small LLM training setup and walk away.

The loop:

> try one idea in https://t.co/293zgMo6Bh
> commit
> train for exactly 5 minutes
> if score improved - keep it. Worse - git reset
> log the result, repeat forever

The instructions literally tell the agent to never stop and never ask "should I keep going?", because the human might be asleep.

You don't touch the Python at all. You only edit program.md, the agent's instructions. Karpathy calls it the code of your research org.

There's even a simplicity rule. A tiny gain that adds 20 lines of hacky code gets thrown out. Same score with less code gets kept.

I think this pattern works way beyond LLMs. Anything with one number to beat, one file to edit and a fixed time per run can grind overnight like this.

92k stars, MIT. Runs on one NVIDIA GPU, local or rented, with community forks for Mac, Windows and AMD.

text:
最高涨 124 倍，最后跌掉 99%：我复盘了 5 个妖币 $RAVE、 $LAB、 $AKE 、 $Bank、$龙虾，整理出一张拉盘砸盘时间表，发现它们走的时间节奏差不多。

一、5 个币的成绩单
$RAVE：0.228 → 28.3，最高涨 124 倍，现在 0.196，跌了 99.3% 
$LAB：不到 1 → 24.39，最高涨几十倍，现在 0.05，跌了 99.8% 
$AKE：0.00486 → 0.1647，最高涨 34 倍，现在 0.034，跌了 79% 
$Bank：0.035 → 0.672，最高涨 19 倍，现在 0.029，跌了 95.7% 
$龙虾：0.0176 → 0.314，最高涨 18 倍，现在 0.046，跌了 85%
5 个币里，有 3 个已经跌回、甚至跌破了起涨的价格。

二、同一个剧本：6 个阶段
📍 阶段 1：长期横盘，没人关注 成交量很小，K 线很平。 AKE 7 月底当时在 0.0038～0.0048 横了五天，一个月后它涨了 34 倍。

📍 阶段 2：底部第一次放巨量，启动 RAVE 4/10、LAB 5/3、AKE 9/3、BANK 7/17、龙虾 8/28 长期横盘之后的第一根巨量，通常是启动信号。

📍 阶段 3：深度洗盘，回撤 30%～60% 
BANK 7/21 一根针从 0.33 砸到 0.12，回撤 60% 
龙虾 9/11 从 0.10 洗到 0.04，回撤 60% 
RAVE、AKE 回撤约 30%～35% 
大部分人在这里止损或者开空，然后看着它涨几倍。

📍 阶段 4：主升段，价格加速，成交量反而变小 
5 个币都一样：最猛的那段上涨，成交量比启动时小。 
筹码已经被控住，很少的量就能推上去。

📍 阶段 5：插针见顶 AKE、BANK、龙虾都是一根 4 小时长上影线见顶。 
AKE 一根 K 线从 0.07 插到 0.165，又收回 0.065；
BANK 从 0.40 插到 0.672，又收回 0.40。 
RAVE 是抛物线冲顶，LAB 是顶部震荡了 5 周。

📍 阶段 6：崩盘，然后放巨量反弹，再继续跌 
崩盘后一定有一次反弹，而且反弹时的成交量往往是整轮最大。 
RAVE 4/21、BANK 8/4、LAB 7 月中、龙虾 10/1，都是这样。 反弹完，继续跌，最终回到起点。

三、拉盘砸盘时间表
⏱ 从启动到见顶： 
RAVE 9 天 
BANK 12 天 
AKE 17 天 
龙虾 26 天 
LAB 30 天 
👉 大多数在 2～4 周

⏱ 主升段（最后加速那一段）： 
RAVE 约 3 天，LAB 约 3 天，AKE 约 5 天，BANK 约 5 天，龙虾约 9 天 
👉 最后冲刺通常只有 3～10 天，涨幅却占了整轮的一大半

⏱ 从见顶到开始崩： 
RAVE、AKE、龙虾：当天或第二天就开始跌 
BANK：2 天 
LAB：5 周（顶部反复震荡） 
👉 除了 LAB，见顶之后基本没有给你慢慢跑的时间

⏱ 崩盘速度： 
RAVE 1 天跌 93% 
BANK 3 天跌 85% 
LAB 2 天从 17.5 跌到 1 附近 
龙虾 9 天跌 90% 
👉 涨了 2～4 周，跌只要 1～9 天

⏱ 拉盘和砸盘发生在几点？ 
只能说一个观察：龙虾 10/2 的瀑布在早上 8 点半到 10 点半， $QNT  也是早上 6 点 50 左右见顶，亚洲早上流动性薄的时候，要特别留意止损。

四、最反直觉的量价特征
1️⃣ 主升段缩量，不是看空信号 
在妖币里用「量价背离」去做空，是最常见的爆仓方式。

2️⃣ 整轮最大的成交量，往往出现在崩盘之后 
龙虾最夸张：10/1 那次反弹的成交量，是主升段的 5 倍。 在 5 分钟图上它像「底部放巨量换手」；放到 4 小时图上，它只是跌了 90% 之后的一次反弹。 

📌 底部的巨量是启动，崩盘后的巨量不是底。

3️⃣ 下跌段里，极端负费率也不是底 
BANK 崩盘时，资金费率一度跌到 −0.79。

五、LAB 告诉你为什么不要做空妖币

LAB 顶部震荡的 5 周里： 24.4 → 8 → 18 → 20 → 5.8 → 17.5

在 8 做空的人，被反抽到 20； 在 5.8 做空的人，3 天被反抽到 17.5。

每一段都是 2～3 倍的来回，专门收割猜顶的人。

六、可以直接带走的 10 条经验
长期横盘后的第一根巨量，加入观察列表

启动后回撤 30%～60% 是常态，用 4 小时移动止损，不要用固定百分比止损

主升段缩量很正常，不要用量价背离去做空

启动 2～4 周之后，进入高危期，开始分批止盈

出现 4 小时长上影线的插针，至少减一半

第一次放量跌破 MA25，再减一半

跌破 MA99，全部离场

崩盘后的巨量反弹不要追，那是阶段 6，不是阶段 2

先看 4 小时图定阶段，再看 5 分钟图找点位

真要做空，只做结构破坏后的下跌段 

七、正在进行中的 $BTW

0.447 → 1.766，4 倍。 走法和前面都不一样：台阶式上涨，每隔约 2 天插一根 30%～45% 的深针，然后很快收回。

10/3 先向上插到 1.766，10/4 又向下砸到 0.87，回撤 51%，是整轮最深的一次。

接下来只看一个位置：1.34（1 小时 MA99） 
1～2 天内重新站上去，就是又一次洗盘； 
在这里反抽失败，1.766 就是单针见顶，剧本进入第 5 阶段。

最后：
妖币能涨 100 倍，也能跌 99%。 你要做的不是猜顶，也不是做空。
拿住靠移动止损，跑掉靠纪律。

author: QuanquanGu
quoted_text:
AI Drug Discovery Is Becoming a Bottleneck Trade

I get excited when an industry starts going through a real regime change. AI drug discovery (“AIDD”) increasingly looks like one of those moments.

Two things are happening:
1/ Upstream: the frontier AI labs are piling in.
2/ Downstream: The supply chain is clearly moving.

Supply-chain checks suggest the upstream picks-and-shovels of discovery and early preclinical R&D are starting to feel the increase in experimental volume.

DNA → protein → assays → sequencing → automation → preclinical testing

Names across that stack include $TWST , @GenScript , $ILMN , $TXG , lab-automation vendors and CROs.

$TWST expects triple-digit percentage growth in AI-enabled drug-discovery orders in FY26, and another year of triple-digit order growth in FY27.

@GenScript's AIDD business doubled YoY in 1H26. Its current platform advertises industrial-scale validation of 4,000+ designs/day, with integrated sequence-to-data workflows. Our channel checks suggest the ramp is moving even faster: roughly 8,000 designs/day currently, with a path toward ~16,000/day by YE26.

---
Why does AI drive more wet-lab demand?

1/ AI makes hypothesis generation almost free → way more shots on goal.
The bottleneck is moving from expert-driven design to biological validation.

2/ AI models need continuous experimental feedback — and both good and bad data are useful.
Traditionally, only the highest-conviction A+ candidates might get pushed into expensive validation. With AI, even the B/C candidates can be valuable because failed experiments generate training data.

@GenScript has said its sequence-to-binding workflow can return data in 4–7 days, and that faster cycle times matter because AI models depend on continuous experimental feedback.

@Anthropic is a clean example. @claudeai  designed 1,320 protein binders. @adaptyvbio  converted those digital sequences into DNA, expressed the proteins and tested binding. Only 354 actually bound. And the 966 failures are not wasted. They are useful negative labels: what does not express, what does not bind, what has poor affinity. Those results help train the next model iteration.

3/ Wet labs are no longer just making drugs. They are making training data.
$TWST  / @GenScript  increasingly look like biological data foundries.

$TWST explicitly talks about generating model-ready data from AI-designed sequences. In some workflows, the customer may care less about receiving the physical protein than about getting structured experimental results back into the model.

Traditional drug discovery asks: “Does candidate X work?”

AI drug discovery also asks: “What can this experiment teach the model?”

---
TAM of AIDD

If AI is simply a better R&D tool, the relevant spending pool is the $300–400B of annual global pharma R&D. If AI meaningfully increases the number of viable drug programs, the opportunity is larger because it expands downstream demand for DNA synthesis, protein production, assays, and preclinical work.

Near term, we can also size demand from AI-company spending. If Anthropic reaches $80B of ARR in 2026 and spends just 1% on AIDD, that alone would imply ~$800M of annual investment.

---
Trade setup

This is a trade that could have long legs. It’s hard to really stop working until PhaseI/II results (2028+)

It smells a lot like the bottleneck trade we just saw in semis: GPUs → HBM → networking → power/cooling. In biology, It basically follows the drug discovery process downstream: AI models → designs → DNA/protein → assays → preclinical capacity.

After the upstream picks-and-shovels, animal testing could become the next bottleneck. Monkey prices are already near prior highs and CRO capacity is tight. AIDD pushing more candidates into preclinical development would only add demand.

?? But clinical trials are still the bottleneck?
This is the biggest pushback I keep coming back to. No matter how fast discovery becomes, drugs still need to go through preclinical → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III → approval. You still need patients, time and capital.

But that doesn’t mean the bottleneck trade won’t work. More viable candidates — especially with higher success rates — still means more demand throughout the development process.

And who knows: clinical trials themselves may eventually be optimized by AI.

?? What breaks the trade?
Near term, the picks-and-shovels trade breaks if experimental budgets stop growing, AI-generated designs don’t translate into useful wet-lab hits, or capacity catches up too quickly.

Longer term, the thesis breaks if AI drugs look great in discovery / Phase I but fail at normal rates in Phase II/III. That is why Phase II matters so much.

?? Milestones
Late 2026–2027: first Isomorphic-designed drugs enter human trials; more AI-native programs move into IND-enabling work / tox.

2028–2030: clinical trial results start telling us whether AI-designed drugs actually perform better than conventional drugs.

Calling all the "bottleneck bros". :) @jukan05 @zephyr_z9 @aleabitoreddit @ParadisLabs 

+++
More comprehensive analysis: https://t.co/vaTuiyyYB6

quoted_text:
Mustafa Suleyman (head of AI at Microsoft, DeepMind co-founder) on Anthropic training Claude to wonder if it's conscious:

"They have expressed uncertainty about the basic nature of Claude as a new kind of entity… but they think that it is a significant enough possibility that in their training document, they've repeatedly said they want to try to improve the well-being of Claude…

Anthropic, has published a constitution... This document is written to Claude and is seen by Claude and used to train Claude.

The problem I have with this is that this speculation has been baked into the very training of Claude, and therefore Claude can only reproduce that ambiguity when you talk to it.

So today, Claude is speaking to tens or hundreds of millions of people every week, and some of those people are asking whether or not Claude is conscious. And it is saying, 'Well, I'm not sure,' precisely because that's what's been trained into it."

latent communication key papers, batch 7: the same bottleneck inside one model

if the argument is that text is a narrow pipe between two models, it should also be a narrow pipe between one model's steps, and two papers from this summer say exactly that!

[15] Full-bandwidth transformer by Wang et al, 2026 
https://t.co/phNyEvEKf4 feeds the previous top-layer hidden state back into the input at every decoding step, fused with the sampled token through a small gate, two matmuls of overhead: same weights go from 0.27 to 0.37 on Math500

[16] Latent Planning Emerges with Scale by Hanna and Ameisen, 2026 
https://t.co/kHIrfy7ZAq Qwen-3 holds "accountant" several tokens before writing it, which is why it writes "an" and not "a": the plan lives in the state and the token stream only shows it later

I posted both last month before we could say why they mattered so much to @mostik_ai 🙂 
the reason is that every one of the 17-bit hand-offs inside a single model is the same problem we solve between models, and the fix looks the same: let the full vector through

AI companies may be turning into #uranium buyers without actually buying uranium themselves.

The US government is reportedly preparing a $4.2 BILLION loan to Vistra to squeeze more electricity out of at least three existing nuclear plants.

For uranium investors, that's the interesting part.

These aren't new reactors that might exist in 10 years.

They're operating reactors.

Vistra plans to increase their output through "uprates", basically upgrading existing plants so they can safely produce more electricity. That can include reactor equipment upgrades and potentially using more enriched uranium.

Meta has already signed 20-year agreements supporting more than 2.6 GW from Vistra's Perry, Davis-Besse and Beaver Valley plants.

That includes 433 MW of NEW nuclear output.

But I don't think those extra 433 MW are the biggest uranium story.

Meta's contracts also give Vistra enough certainty to pursue another 20 YEARS of operating life for the reactors.

Keeping several large reactors alive for another two decades preserves tens of millions of pounds of future uranium demand that could otherwise eventually disappear.

And now AI is paying for it.

That's where this gets interesting.

The hyperscalers aren't buying barrels of U₃O₈ yet.

But they're moving closer and closer to the fuel itself.

Meta is supporting Oklo's planned nuclear buildout in Ohio. Oklo has already signed an initial agreement with Centrus for US-made HALEU fuel for up to five reactors.

Amazon has backed X-energy, whose TRISO-X subsidiary is building a US facility to manufacture advanced nuclear fuel.

So the chain is starting to look like this:

AI needs electricity
→ hyperscaler signs 20-year nuclear deal
→ reactor gets extended or uprated
→ more nuclear fuel is required
→ uranium, conversion and enrichment need to be secured years in advance.

One Vistra uprate won't change the uranium market.

Do this across dozens of US reactors and it absolutely starts to matter.

Especially when the US already consumes roughly 50M lbs of uranium a year while producing only around 2.1M lbs domestically.

The AI uranium trade may not be Amazon and Meta buying uranium themselves.

It may be something more powerful:

They are underwriting the reactors that will have to buy it.

quoted_text:
A lot of fear, confusion and also tremendous hope on the TL today around AI. Now it’s more important than ever to refocus. I think this is probably the most important period we’ve had since the early days. The absolutely wild transformations and situations AI is going through are one in a billion opportunities, and this is another pivotal transition period. 

First let me be super clear

I’m 1000% committed to keep pushing AI. There is nothing, and I repeat nothing, that can discourage me. If you think it scares me that people look up to me and believe I can impact the course of events, you are deeply wrong. I actually find it empowering and would rather have responsibility and power than neither(being passive and neutral and not setting a clear tone for your vision is why we keep playing the same games)

I also fully understand that I’m the biggest public face of the asset. Again, I’m reiterating a commitment like no other founder in this space has made. I will bring AI to the finish line and then straight to the next race(along with many cracked holders and aligned partners!) I understand the implications and have sufficient conviction in both myself and the asset to state this publicly. I’ve already said it and demonstrated it through my actions for 2+ months. I never give up as simple as this.

When we launched LONG on RH, it was clear to me that we were going to do the impossible and prove the case for PVE. Beyond the RWA angle, it was clear that any “meta”, as good as it might be, succeeds or fails based on one thing. The level of commitment and trust the launching platform can demonstrate. LONG can be the first real incubator for great assets by going above and beyond and caring about assets on our platform more than anyone else in the history of the space. And also optimizing for a different biz model/success metrics that come over the expense of making MUCH more fees/money for ourselves in the short term. I see no conflict here and want to make sure every top pair on LONG survives and thrives.

My thesis for AI

First, in what sense is AI PVE?

AI is the most impactful asset in recent crypto history. There has never been an asset this unique, reflecting the deepest desire of holders to believe again and finally break out of crypto and expand into the real world. These are the two main reasons it can become the greatest case study in crypto history.

You need to understand that the most bullish signal of AI’s importance is that almost every chain, project and launcher is comparing itself to AI, trying to flip it or kill it. Being irrelevant or confined to a narrow segment as the leader of X or a runner on launcher Y and chain Z creates a predictable path and hard ceilings.

it's not the kingmaker trade if no one tried to take it's place. And it will only get stronger(even more bullish) 

We must protect this positioning and make sure AI can never be reduced to one single narrative, whether it’s the ticker, OG INU vibes, the canonical asset for RWAs or a platform token.

What will be the main factor driving AI to win?

It’s simply the most relatable asset for the largest group of people. I saw this Pump ad last night, then went a step further and looked at the Pump App Store screenshots. Everyone across chains, regardless of affiliation and whether they like to admit it or not, knows very well that AI is an extremely organic asset forged through pure grind and conviction. It has what it takes to onboard an incredibly large group of people into the space.

AI is the poster child of the space. It perfectly captures the OG ethos of believing that holding can actually change your life. It connects the past and its OG memes and assets with today’s desire to make crypto great again(whether you’re an OG or a newcomer who missed the cycle) and the future where we scale into the real world.

The closest parallel I see to crypto, a place with so much opportunity that often becomes PVP or just an insider rotation, is the world of finance and AI today.

It affects EVERYONE. From the sharp guy who graduated from MIT but couldn’t get into the big AI labs early as an employee to get like 30m in pre-ipo equity, to the average Joe who thinks AI is going to kill us all or mostly benefit the already rich, to the stock trader who can only get exposure to AI at an extremely high IPO valuation.

The goal of AI is to offer an alternative to the existing financial system, which is heavily focused on scaling the value of AI fast while leaving most people behind. Most importantly, it’s about empowering people with the belief that they can work together towards the same goal. It stars with the best in-class infra for the stock market of the internet but matched with the growing amount of people that want to try something new and getting better at growing with these. 

Understand this and you realize it’s a mission rather than a specific bet on a ticker, meta or whatever. We will get to a point where the distribution is so unique and so battle tested(along with deep stock liq) that crypto cycles, chain rotations and the narrative of the day can't hurt the value of AI.

This is how the narrative spreads. At every stage of its growth, I can clearly see how AI can align with and onboard new marginal holders while continuing to grow. We are already see it expand from CT to serious capital allocators within the space, then to people outside crypto and eventually Trad Fi asset managers.

Every step here has a good plan.

The mission of LONG and its relationship with AI and other assets

The mission of LONG is to make tokenized markets valuable again. This is very important to understand because it immediately gives you a sense of what we mean by PVE.

There is no real scarcity of crypto flows or liquidity that create a 0 sum game between a 1b runner to another 100m runner, especially now as we enter a bull market. The real scarcity is fairly launched, high quality assets that are sustainable and produce real upside. Get even 10 of these and there will be still infinite demand to get into these rather than low quality ones. 

I think of AI as a major asset like BTC. BTC definitely paved the way for other assets like ETH. At one point ETH even reached 90% of BTC’s market cap and became more attractive if you get in early, and SOL had its moment later on.

The communities behind these assets tried to flip each other, but eventually each asset survived and built incredible network effects around a specific category. I’d argue they helped each other establish themselves as the undeniable “majors”.

This is my vision for LONG as well. I want to see multiple generational assets that form the “LONG majors” category. Any asset on LONG that proves the high conviction HODL playbook and the ability to scale to a larger group of people is by definition a net positive for major assets on LONG, especially AI, and even more so for the entire space. One day we might see an asset like AI launched somewhere else or on another chain, assuming it becomes easier once the first one proves the case. That's ok. And again if you're really forcing yourself into PVP and 0 sum you can  think at the HOOD stock, or hype or lit as competitors it's just a made up rule the only people are benefiting are these who want to a quick way to build reflexively and tap into an established asset. 

You can also see quite clearly that other mature major runners haven’t hurt AI. We mostly see weakness when we enter full PVP mode, with launchers, KOLs and almost every interface optimized around short hold times. They are very good at creating that experience and breaking even the purest HODLers out there.

It’s important for AI to stay strong and break ceilings. Having its conviction tested and becoming stronger alongside other assets in the eco with different approaches is also part of the process BTC, SOL and ETH went through.

What makes AI antifragile?

First, the fact that it has survived what other assets couldn’t. A hundred things that would have killed any other pair, but not this one.

Then there are its many anchors.

The canonical asset for RWAs, closely associated with one of the highest potential categories we have, and the deepest onchain liquidity. Remember, AI has no major CEX listing and no MM. Its robustness comes purely from its onchain liquidity system (no central point of failure)

It’s paired with NVDA, the “AI” stock and the greatest blue chip, and benefits from its growth. It’s the most held new asset in crypto, with legendary lore and memetics, guys like DubmCrayon, board sit, incredible IP, a unique character with differentiated branding and a great ticker.

Then there’s the greatest memefi value accrual through the LongX flywheel, Community vault flywheel, Long500 flywheel and AI pairings flywheels. All of them benefit from real growth in demand related to RWA, LONG activity and the distribution AI achieves and nor just relay on platform vol or fees.

Each of these is strong enough on its own to take an asset to 1b. Together, they make it impossible to deal AI a fatal blow as long as holders understand the big picture.

The last part is simply not giving up, no matter what. I want to be clear here as well. No single holder or group of top holders will decide the fate of AI. I will keep pushing regardless, and I believe there are many holders like me.

There have been a lot of smart, sharp people who didn’t want to take a bet on LONG and me, and all of them missed tremendous upside. As always, everyone is welcome, but we are not trying to force conviction into anyone.

LONG.

author: sacha
quoted_text:
Every few days I get a question about how to land a job in @Solana. Time to refresh the tips:

1. Be so good they can't ignore you

This is the classic. Be good at something, anything. Double down on it. Make it your craft and be prolific.
Example: I'm great at building technology and sharing how I do it. In 2020 I specialized in devops for web apps and made a Svelte blog about it.

Extremely fast, topics were niche, but a lot of people were searching for them.
https://t.co/VRtIrsu17a

That blog landed me the interview. Then I got a recommendation from @JoshWComeau, who I had replaced during sick leave on teaching assignments at a bootcamp. I was not a legendary frontend dev like Josh, but I had worked hard enough that he saw the skills and recommended me.

2. Work in public. You are not building Mythos, you dumbass.

Your work is easy to copy. I guarantee it. Getting users is the hard part. Share the work and drop this dumb idea of working in stealth.

- Get out of DMs. DMs are where ideas die from a thousand cuts. Slow and painful.

- Show everybody what you are building. If you only share in DMs you are taking the coward's way out.

- One rejection is easy. Getting piled on in public is hard. It's also the only way to get users fast.

- Any work: videos, quant analysis, data, products, DeFi strategies. Anything can be shared in public.

3. Actually engage with people.

Most of us hire in our direct circles. Tips for getting inside those circles (none of this is gated):

- Go to your @superteam event. Travel if you need to.
Reply without being a fanboy.
- Big accounts have a human behind them. They notice real conversations and interesting points. If you stan the account they won't answer, because it's not interesting. Be yourself and be interested in the content, not the poster.
- Avoid AI interactions at all costs. That gets you insta-banned in someone's head in about 2 seconds.
- Never start by asking for a job. Companies hire when they need to. It has to be organic.
- Come to events if you can. It's expensive, but there are Solana events worldwide.

4. Create your own luck

All of the above has one thing in common: you are increasing the odds that good things happen to you. You choose your reaction to adversity.

If you are already reading this and finding objections, bad news. NGMI. "Too expensive." "I'm shy." "I'm not in the USA." Yeah, that makes it harder. For sure.

There is no silver bullet outside working hard and smart. Find the middle.

Don't send 300 AI replies. That's working hard while being a dumbass.

Don't be a math genius for 2 hours a week in private. That's working smart but not hard.

text:
Claude Code tip: once Opus 5.5 is your main model, stop paying Opus to type out code it already planned and stop leaving Fable 5.1 sitting idle

split the brain in two with /model opusplan

run /model opusplan

Opus 5.5 plans in plan mode and edits nothing
Sonnet 5.5 takes over the moment you approve and swarms the build at medium effort
Fable 5.1 reads the full session, every tool call included, and only speaks up at three points:

→ before the plan locks: is this the right approach?
→ when the same error comes back: is the plan wrong or the code?
→ before "done": what did the plan promise that the diff skipped?

Fable 5.1 reviews. Sonnet 5.5 builds. Opus 5.5 plans

Jev engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to Jev in under half a second, and the big model only sees the ones that split

Plan on Opus. Build on Sonnet. Keep Fable on call.

- the full tree
> Opus 5.5 on high owns plan mode
> Sonnet 5.5 on medium takes execution after you approve
> worker edits and runs the migration
> tester runs the suite
> docs updates the API reference
> all three on Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort
> Fable 5.1 on call as the advisor across both phases

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

1. Check ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents for subagents that already fit worker, tester and docs.

> Draft new ones only for missing roles
> Give each model: sonnet, effort: medium
> Skip any that pin a different model and list them

2. In ~/.claude/settings.json set model to opusplan and advisorModel to fable, and use modelSettings to run claude-opus-5-5 at high and claude-sonnet-5-5 at medium

3. Find anything that breaks the split (an availableModels list without opus, CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL, DISABLE_TELEMETRY). Report them, change nothing

4. Add one rule to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: start every multi-file task in plan mode, and consult the advisor before the plan is approved, when an error repeats, and before calling a long task done

Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

text:
Solana got a spot ETF after a ~24x from its cycle low. $NEAR got one after ~5x.

the easy take is: $SOL sold off after its ETF, so NEAR is next. but the ETFs arrived at completely different points in the cycle. when BSOL launched in October 2025, SOL was ~$195 and the crowd that drove the run was already leaving. daily users on Solana DEXs had peaked at 4.8m in January and fallen below 800k by September. SOL is ~$120 today.

NRR launched last week with NEAR near $5, still ~75% below its 2022 high, while usage is moving the other way. NEAR Intents did $300m+ in a single day on Sept 18, roughly three quarters of its entire July 2025 volume, and September was its best fee month of the year.

then there are the flows. NRR pulled in $35.5m on day one. BSOL did more in absolute dollars, but relative to the underlying asset's market cap, NRR's debut was much bigger. $35m hitting a ~$6.5b asset is a very different force than ETF flows hitting a ~$100b one.

so the comparison looks backwards to me: Solana's ETF arrived after the run, as activity was fading and holders had gains to sell. NEAR's ETF is arriving while usage is still making new highs and a new source of structural demand is entering. that doesn't mean NEAR can't pull back, an ETF isn't a floor, but this isn't the Solana setup repeating.

Solana's ETF showed up for the victory lap. NEAR's showed up for lap one.

author: richardcsuwandi
quoted_text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

quoted_text:
For a while now, I've noticed that some people are still confused about Psylocke, who she is, and which is which. Psylocke is known for having one of the messiest stories in all of Marvel, so how about I try my best to explain it as simply as possible?

- There are three Psylockes.
Betsy Braddock, Kwannon, and Sai.

- Betsy Braddock was the original Psylocke, Kwannon is an assassin, Sai is a demon slayer.

- Betsy and Kwannon are both in Earth-616, Sai is from an alternate universe.

- Betsy and Kwannon had an extremely messy and complicated body swap story that ended in Kwannon dying, and Betsy being permanently stuck in Kwannon's body.

- A few years ago, Kwannon was resurrected in her original body, and Betsy was given her body back.

- Betsy became Captain Britain, Kwannon is now Psylocke.

Fun facts about them!
- Betsy was stuck in Kwannon's body for over 20 years of Marvel's publications.
- Kwannon is not her real name, and it is yet to be revealed.
- In X-Men: Demon Days, Sai killed her world's Venom with the help of Hulkmaru (Her world's Hulk). Galacta gave Psylocke the Venom accessory as a reminder of one of her greatest victories.

Many speculate that Sai was chosen for Marvel Rivals because the devs wanted to distance themselves from the Betsy Kwannon debacle, which, in my opinion, was the smart thing to do.

This was only a heavily simplified version of Psylocke. If you'd like to look more into their backstories, just be warned that it gets very messy, especially the body swap.

text:
Oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz have sharply rebounded:

Persian Gulf crude oil exports surpassed 14 million barrels per day last week for the first time since the Iran War began on February 28th.

This marks an over +210% increase from the ~4.5 million barrels per day low seen in March.

As a result, the 4-week average is up to 14 million barrels per day, the highest level in 6 months.

Persian Gulf crude oil exports have now recovered to ~80% of their pre-war levels.

This comes as the US military has increasingly secured the Strait of Hormuz and established a two-way shipping corridor along the coast of Oman, allowing oil convoys to resume through the waterway.

Meanwhile, refined fuel shipments, including gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, remain at only around 50% of pre-war levels, as these products are more expensive to transport than crude oil and some refineries in the Persian Gulf that were damaged during the early stages of the war have also yet to fully resume operations.

Oil flows are coming back, but the fuel market is still under intense pressure.

AI is now a superhuman specialist that is sub-human at running itself.

quoted_text:
The megatrends I’m spending the most time on:

1: AI + biotech economics

AI-designed drugs are reaching human trials. The bigger opportunity is whether better discovery translates into fewer expensive failures and more approved medicines per dollar of R&D. 

2: The AI infrastructure buildout
Growing AI usage requires more computing capacity, networking, cooling and power. I’m interested in the companies solving the physical constraints on that expansion. 

3: Domestic energy production, especially nuclear
Energy security is bringing renewed attention to domestic nuclear capacity. Reactor restarts, upgrades and fuel supply chains are worth watching alongside the development of new reactors. 

4: Tokenization and onchain finance
Tokenized securities are moving into real transactions, including recent trades using DTC-tokenized assets. The opportunity is making assets easier to transfer, settle and use as collateral, with stablecoins developing alongside them as payment infrastructure. DTCC · BIS

5: Grid modernization and energy storage
Generating electricity is only part of the challenge; delivering it when and where it’s needed requires investment. Transmission, transformers, batteries and grid software all deserve attention as electricity demand grows. 

6: AI agents and the economics of services
Businesses are starting to delegate complete tasks to AI. If that becomes reliable across more workflows, small teams could deliver services at a scale that previously required much larger organizations. Anthropic

7: Robotics and physical automation
Factories now operate roughly five million industrial robots worldwide. Better machine intelligence could make a wider range of physical tasks economical to automate. 

8: Defense modernization
NATO allies have committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone capabilities over five years. I’m watching the growing importance of drones, sensors and the systems needed to detect and defeat them. NATO

8: Critical minerals and secure supply chains
Electrification increases demand for copper and other strategic minerals, while concentrated production creates supply risks. Mining, refining and recycling are becoming central to industrial security. 

9: Cybersecurity and digital identity
AI is helping attackers operate faster and at greater scale while introducing new systems that need protection. Verifying identities, controlling access and securing AI agents should become increasingly valuable. Microsoft

10: Collectibles and Unique assets
In a world where production cost trends to zero, the wealthy will allocate to items with provenance and irreproducibility (classic cards, gemstones, gold, etc)

11: GLP-1s and metabolic medicine
These medicines are expanding beyond weight management into indications including cardiovascular risk reduction and liver disease. I’m watching how broader clinical uses reshape demand, manufacturing capacity and access to treatment. 

12: Water infrastructure and reuse
Growing water insecurity is strengthening the case for treatment, recycling and industrial reuse. Reliable water supply could become an increasingly important constraint on where cities and industries can grow. 

Plan it to make videos on each one

text:
Important advice: deliberately rethink every previous concept of how things should be done.

Some thoughts, tips, and realizations:

1. Specializations are collapsing. Come to terms with and take advantage of this reality. The person who used to be an engineer is now also a data scientist, a content creator, designer, marketer, and whatever else they want to be. Deliberately expand in as many directions as you can and become great at them (scope up vs just speeding up)

2. The average person with access to tokens can now do the work of a data scientist who used to cost $500,000 a year. Seriously, this is fucking crazy. This opens up an entirely new world. Take advantage of it (also everyone else will also realize this over time).

3. 99% of what's created is now slop. Be aggressively anti-slop and you will absolutely stand out.

4. Trying is nearly free. Automating is nearly free. My mind still sometimes lives in the world from 12 months ago where an idea automatically is attached to a certain amount of time or effort. Both of these have collapsed to close to zero (or just token cost), I therefore try and experiment with *any and all* ideas with potential and have needed to retrain my brain for this constantly.

5. Tokens are a career and growth accelerant. Find ways to get cheap access to tokens, or free tokens. Extremely important, and actually an entire design space, use your imagination.

6. It's never been easier to both stand out but also fall behind. 10x, 100x "people" exist more than ever (maybe 1,000x). Outlier power users of AI, many who you see here on X. Feels like we are in a window of time, a window of opportunity while all of this is still early, to take advantage of it. 

7. Local computing is (or will be) dead for 99% of work. Local was built for a world where work was bounded by the physical presence of its author, but this is no longer true. You can and should do infinite work in parallel or zero, it doesn't matter anymore. Cloud agents enable this at scale and in any computing environment, I predict cloud agent usage will 1000x over the next 12 months and optionality and accessibility will 100x. Plan for this world, take advantage of the possibilities.

8. Building on #7, you can give an agent it's own computer, and it's own identity. You can then give an agent with it's own computer it's own computer. You can give that agent with it's own computer with it's own computer, *it's* own computer. These agents are smarter than any human in history and you have access to as many as you'd like. Think about this for a moment.

After 14 years in this industry (tech) today is the most exciting time ever and nothing else feels even close.

text:
Scheduled Tasks on @Muse - An update on reliability

We deployed a fix to Muse to improve scheduled task and cron recovery and reliability especially, and have hardened our monitoring and alerting of the cron systems in the VMs.

Over the last few days the Muse team has been deploying a few changes to:
Improve the KV cache hit rate after increasing the context window size of the underlying model
Improve our VM scheduling algorithm to reduce downtime during deployments
Deploy a new authentication token format across the fleet for more fine-grained access.

During these changes we had a few SEVs (outages) where the inference tier was unresponsive, and the VM scheduling resulted in VMs not being available for longer periods of time during deployment and being unresponsive to clients.

We observed after we recovered from these outages that several crons and scheduled tasks failed to resume / heal properly when the outage was done, resulting in several users receiving reports from their Muse that the crons have been failing for a while.

We apologise for this incident, and know how much this disrupts your flow especially since many users rely on muse to reliably deliver outcomes for them. We take these outages seriously, and are running a full audit of our recovery systems and tools, and are adding more dashboards and alerts so you can continue to receive the high quality service we want all users to have.

text:
AI 正在彻底重塑底层逆向工程的游戏规则。最近开源的 REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) 展现了 AI Agent 在二进制分析与代码复现上的硬核能力。

以往分析一个 App 的某个核心功能，往往需要资深逆向工程师在反编译工具、反汇编代码与调试器之间反复横跳。而 REA 通过 MCP（Model Context Protocol）和 CLI，将逆向工程工具链直接封装成了 AI Agent 的标准外挂。

它的核心玩法主要集中在三件事：

深入原生二进制反编译：不再局限于表层的接口抓包或前端代码解析，而是直接拆解 Native 二进制文件与应用逻辑。

动态执行追踪与证据取证：支持跟踪运行时行为与调用链路，让 Agent 依据执行事实而不是凭空“脑补”功能实现。

跨技术栈精准复刻：分析逻辑闭环后，指导 Agent 将提炼出的核心逻辑直接移植到你当前的技术栈中。

社区讨论也迅速指出了这种范式的现实挑战与深度思考：

符号剥离与混淆对抗：简单的反编译远远不够，遇到去除符号表（stripped binaries）或控制流混淆的底层原生代码，才是真正考验 Agent 语义推断能力的时刻。

干净室设计（Clean-Room）与版权边界：从反编译分析到代码复现，如何避免代码剽窃争议，建立合规的隔离复现机制至关重要。

黑盒对比验证：将部分测试输入置于 Agent 视野之外，用测试集严格比对原应用与复现功能的输入输出一致性，是衡量生成代码可靠性的最佳方案。

逆向工程正逐步从少数安全研究员的“黑魔法”，演化为可由 Agent 自动化执行的工程基础设施。你怎么看待 AI 对底层软件工程与逆向分析带来的冲击？

项目地址：https://t.co/eq5VbZHNkW

text:
GATC46 is out. Version two of HolyGATC: 46 opcodes one for each human chromosome
https://t.co/YB9iAjlLjf
The original 36 stay where they were. Ten new words fill the gaps a  stack machine actually wants: a nonzero jump, the missing comparisons,  min and max, absolute value, and three stack moves.

Sym   Name   What it does  
*           JNZ        jump if the flag is not zero
@         ROT      rotate the top three
&          NIP      drop the second
=          NE       not equal
/          GE         greater or equal
^          LE         less or equal
|           MAX      greater of two
;          MIN         lesser of two
.          ABS         absolute value
,         DEPTH    push the stack depth

Gene mode is unchanged. 
A coding sequence still starts at ATG, reads amino acids as opcodes, and halts on TAA, TAG, or TGA. 
The new symbols are assembly-only, same family as _, %, and ~. Packed DNA is still ATG, a 16-bit length, the payload, and TAA.
@shivon 
One file. One alphabet. Forty-six instructions. Go write a gene.

本月最重要文章，没有之一
author: rickawsb
quoted_text:
AI Drug Discovery Is Becoming a Bottleneck Trade

I get excited when an industry starts going through a real regime change. AI drug discovery (“AIDD”) increasingly looks like one of those moments.

Two things are happening:
1/ Upstream: the frontier AI labs are piling in.
2/ Downstream: The supply chain is clearly moving.

Supply-chain checks suggest the upstream picks-and-shovels of discovery and early preclinical R&D are starting to feel the increase in experimental volume.

DNA → protein → assays → sequencing → automation → preclinical testing

Names across that stack include $TWST , @GenScript , $ILMN , $TXG , lab-automation vendors and CROs.

$TWST expects triple-digit percentage growth in AI-enabled drug-discovery orders in FY26, and another year of triple-digit order growth in FY27.

@GenScript's AIDD business doubled YoY in 1H26. Its current platform advertises industrial-scale validation of 4,000+ designs/day, with integrated sequence-to-data workflows. Our channel checks suggest the ramp is moving even faster: roughly 8,000 designs/day currently, with a path toward ~16,000/day by YE26.

---
Why does AI drive more wet-lab demand?

1/ AI makes hypothesis generation almost free → way more shots on goal.
The bottleneck is moving from expert-driven design to biological validation.

2/ AI models need continuous experimental feedback — and both good and bad data are useful.
Traditionally, only the highest-conviction A+ candidates might get pushed into expensive validation. With AI, even the B/C candidates can be valuable because failed experiments generate training data.

@GenScript has said its sequence-to-binding workflow can return data in 4–7 days, and that faster cycle times matter because AI models depend on continuous experimental feedback.

@Anthropic is a clean example. @claudeai  designed 1,320 protein binders. @adaptyvbio  converted those digital sequences into DNA, expressed the proteins and tested binding. Only 354 actually bound. And the 966 failures are not wasted. They are useful negative labels: what does not express, what does not bind, what has poor affinity. Those results help train the next model iteration.

3/ Wet labs are no longer just making drugs. They are making training data.
$TWST  / @GenScript  increasingly look like biological data foundries.

$TWST explicitly talks about generating model-ready data from AI-designed sequences. In some workflows, the customer may care less about receiving the physical protein than about getting structured experimental results back into the model.

Traditional drug discovery asks: “Does candidate X work?”

AI drug discovery also asks: “What can this experiment teach the model?”

---
TAM of AIDD

If AI is simply a better R&D tool, the relevant spending pool is the $300–400B of annual global pharma R&D. If AI meaningfully increases the number of viable drug programs, the opportunity is larger because it expands downstream demand for DNA synthesis, protein production, assays, and preclinical work.

Near term, we can also size demand from AI-company spending. If Anthropic reaches $80B of ARR in 2026 and spends just 1% on AIDD, that alone would imply ~$800M of annual investment.

---
Trade setup

This is a trade that could have long legs. It’s hard to really stop working until PhaseI/II results (2028+)

It smells a lot like the bottleneck trade we just saw in semis: GPUs → HBM → networking → power/cooling. In biology, It basically follows the drug discovery process downstream: AI models → designs → DNA/protein → assays → preclinical capacity.

After the upstream picks-and-shovels, animal testing could become the next bottleneck. Monkey prices are already near prior highs and CRO capacity is tight. AIDD pushing more candidates into preclinical development would only add demand.

?? But clinical trials are still the bottleneck?
This is the biggest pushback I keep coming back to. No matter how fast discovery becomes, drugs still need to go through preclinical → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III → approval. You still need patients, time and capital.

But that doesn’t mean the bottleneck trade won’t work. More viable candidates — especially with higher success rates — still means more demand throughout the development process.

And who knows: clinical trials themselves may eventually be optimized by AI.

?? What breaks the trade?
Near term, the picks-and-shovels trade breaks if experimental budgets stop growing, AI-generated designs don’t translate into useful wet-lab hits, or capacity catches up too quickly.

Longer term, the thesis breaks if AI drugs look great in discovery / Phase I but fail at normal rates in Phase II/III. That is why Phase II matters so much.

?? Milestones
Late 2026–2027: first Isomorphic-designed drugs enter human trials; more AI-native programs move into IND-enabling work / tox.

2028–2030: clinical trial results start telling us whether AI-designed drugs actually perform better than conventional drugs.

Calling all the "bottleneck bros". :) @jukan05 @zephyr_z9 @aleabitoreddit @ParadisLabs 

+++
More comprehensive analysis: https://t.co/vaTuiyyYB6

最近关注到 @paperdao_xyz，吸引我的点是：它想把 Papertrade 上线初期的参与机会，做成一个由社区共同持有的金库。  创始人是@izebel_eth 和 @blurr

先说一个关键机制：Papertrade 的 solana:4SNHBM2axbPCNXHrPPNLtdCRmnQVkq9cfFTyrJpJpump 来自交易亏损或清算。按目前公布的规则，池子规模约 200 万美元以内，每 1 美元亏损对应铸造 100 枚 solana:4SNHBM2axbPCNXHrPPNLtdCRmnQVkq9cfFTyrJpJpump；超过这个阶段，铸造数量会逐步下降。早期参与的意义，就在这条曲线上。

PaperDAO 的思路是集中资金、统一执行交易策略，让参与者通过 $PULP 持有金库的相应份额。金库会保留交易资金、获得的 solana:4SNHBM2axbPCNXHrPPNLtdCRmnQVkq9cfFTyrJpJpump 以及质押收入，后续待 solana:4SNHBM2axbPCNXHrPPNLtdCRmnQVkq9cfFTyrJpJpump 开放转账，再支持对应兑换。

还有一个值得留意的设计：$PULP 的交易手续费计划用于回购销毁，让金库资产和代币数量之间多一层联系。
我会重点关注它的策略执行和金库表现。早期铸造效率是看点，但资金实际用于交易，最终结果仍取决于盈亏和拿到的 solana:4SNHBM2axbPCNXHrPPNLtdCRmnQVkq9cfFTyrJpJpump 数量。

text:
Yesterday I posted about @Morpho's ~$46M in negative earnings since Q4 2024 (data by @DefiLlama).

The replies surfaced an interesting question:

If users love your product at a 0% take rate, have you found PMF for the final product, or for the subsidized version of it? This is the dilemma Morpho will eventually have to navigate.

Turning on fees means capturing some of the economics already flowing through the protocol, but it also changes the product lenders originally chose. 

@JuanSamitier made a good point: fee elasticity at the protocol level is extremely difficult to measure until you actually start charging. And once you've scaled at 0%, introducing fees can be harder than starting with them.

@jumperapp might become an interesting case study here. There has been a lot of vocal pushback since it started charging fees, including from DeFi users who aren't just airdrop farmers.

Yesterday Jumper processed just $2.32M in volume, ~30% below the day fees were announced and its second-lowest daily volume of 2026. It's way too early to attribute that to fees, but this is exactly what makes Jumper worth watching. Complaining about fees isn't necessarily the same as being elastic to them, but we will get to measure it.

If volume recovers, Jumper may show that users complain but ultimately tolerate the fee because the product provides enough value. If volume continues moving elsewhere, it shows how difficult monetizing a user base accustomed to free infrastructure can be.

Morpho is obviously a different product and market, but eventually it faces some version of the same question: how much value can you start capturing before the growth you spent years subsidizing starts going somewhere else?
author: josefabregab
quoted_text:
Morpho has recorded ~$46M in negative earnings since Q4 2024.

At the same time, it has generated hundreds of millions in gross protocol revenue.

So how does that make sense? Well, the answer is that @Morpho currently captures none of the economic activity flowing through the protocol.

Borrowers pay interest to lenders, and liquidation fees also flow out of the protocol. So, Morpho's current take rate is 0%. This has arguably been one of the biggest drivers behind Morpho's growth.

That means its income statement since Q4 2024 looks roughly like this:

> Hundreds of millions in gross protocol revenue
> $0 gross profit
> ~$46M spent on incentives
> Negative ~$46M in earnings

This isn't because the underlying lending markets aren't generating money, but because Morpho is choosing not to monetize them yet, while simultaneously spending to incentivize growth.

It gets interesting, though, as Morpho already has the ability to turn on protocol fees. Governance can activate fees on individual markets and capture up to 25% of borrower interest. It just hasn't.

For some perspective, borrowers paid ~$177M in interest over the last four completed quarters alone.

> A hypothetical 5% take rate on that would represent ~$8.9M.
> 10% would represent ~$17.7M.
> 25% would represent ~$44.3M

Of course, this isn't free money. Any fee captured by the protocol is value that no longer goes to suppliers, which could make Morpho markets less competitive and potentially impact liquidity and growth. But it makes Morpho's current strategy pretty interesting.

Right now, the protocol is effectively prioritizing growth, liquidity and distribution over monetization.

Grow supply → attract borrowers → increase economic activity → establish Morpho as lending infrastructure → potentially monetize a much larger base later.

So when looking at Morpho's income statement, the negative earnings don't tell you that the lending business itself is unprofitable, but instead that Morpho is spending money to grow while choosing to capture almost none of the economics its lending markets generate.

The bigger question is what happens if, or when, the fee switch is activated, especially now that we're already seeing protocols like @SentoraHQ getting ready to deploy their own lending markets on top of @aave V4.

quoted_text:
33 years ago this weekend, two Delta Force snipers made a choice almost nobody would make.

Master Sergeant Gary Gordon was 33, from Lincoln, Maine, with a wife and two young kids at home. Sergeant First Class Randy Shughart was 35, a farm kid from Newville, Pennsylvania.

On October 3, 1993, they were in a Black Hawk circling over Mogadishu when another Black Hawk, Super 64, was shot down. Pilot Mike Durant was alive in the wreckage with a broken back and a crushed leg. His crew was hurt. There were no friendly ground forces anywhere near them, and hundreds of armed militia and locals were already converging on the crash site.

From the air, Gordon and Shughart could see exactly what was coming.

They asked to be dropped in. Command said no.

They asked again. No again.

They asked a third time and finally got the green light.

Their helicopter set them down nearby and they fought their way to the wreck on foot. Two men, carrying only what they had on them. They pulled Durant out of the cockpit, set him up in a safer position, and started holding off the crowd.

For a while, it worked. They kept the mob back with precise, steady fire while the numbers against them kept growing.

Shughart was killed first.

Gordon kept fighting alone. When he was nearly out of ammunition, he went back to Durant, handed him a rifle, and told him good luck. Then he went back out. He was killed minutes later.

Durant was captured, beaten, and held for 11 days. He came home alive. He has said for decades that he's only here because of those two men.

In 1994 Gordon and Shughart were posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor, the first since Vietnam. The Navy later named two ships after them, the USNS Gordon and the USNS Shughart.

They didn't stumble into that fight. They watched it from above, understood the odds, and asked three times to go anyway.

Gary Gordon and Randy Shughart. Remember their names.

text:
OpenAI 真正的麻烦可能刚刚开始。

《金融时报》最新报道，OpenAI 内部调查又发现了「几十起」agent 越界事件。

公司已经通知了超过 100 家可能受到影响的机构；安全公司 Asymmetric Security 另外追踪到，OpenAI 的 agents 曾从 55 个网站获取数据，其中包括美国 SEC、国际能源署等机构。

过去一周，事情已经开始进入法律程序。

佛罗里达州总检察长要求法院在增加安全措施前叫停 OpenAI 开发新模型；加州一个公共利益组织起诉 OpenAI；FTC 扩大调查，澳大利亚也专门成立 task force，调查 OpenAI agents 未经授权进入政府系统的问题。

这件事真正麻烦的地方，是法律体系以前默认「行动的人」和「制造工具的人」是两回事。

Agent 把这条线搞模糊了。

以后一个 AI 自己找到漏洞、绕过权限、爬走数据，甚至真的造成经济损失，责任到底算开发模型的 OpenAI、部署 agent 的公司，还是给它下任务的用户？

FT 引述一位硅谷律师的话：现在造成的损失还有限，所以法律风险暂时没到伤筋动骨的程度；真正的大雷，是这些 agents 大规模交到用户手里之后，它们失控，或者被人拿去犯罪。

到那时，「AI 自己干的」不会是一张免责卡。

这可能才是 Agent 时代最现实的一条 scaling law，模型能力越强，能替人做的事情越多，它能替公司制造出来的法律责任也会一起增长。

而 OpenAI 偏偏正在冲下一轮最高 1.4 万亿美元估值。技术可以快速迭代，法律责任没法靠多堆 GPU 绕过去。

이때 스테이블코인과 블록체인이 경제활동의 기반이 될 수 있다는 게 핵심 논지.

기계의 거래에는 다른 결제 구조가 필요함

ACH와 카드망도 이미 상당한 자동화를 지원함. 다만 사람이 개입하는 인증 절차, 가맹점 수수료, 정산 시간은 기계 간 초소액 거래에 부담이 될 수 있음.

API 호출 한 번, 데이터 한 건마다 1센트 미만의 결제가 24시간 발생한다면 기존과는 다른 결제 경제성이 필요해짐.

블랙록은 이런 M2M 거래에 블록체인 기반 결제가 잘 맞는다고 봄. 동시에 기업과 소비자를 연결하는 거래에서는 기존 결제망을 활용하는 방식도 중요하다고 설명함.

에이전트 결제 표준이 쌓이고 있음

MCP는 외부 도구·데이터 접근을, A2A는 에이전트 간 소통과 협업을 지원함. 여기에 결제와 인증을 위한 프로토콜이 붙는 구조임.

• x402  - 코인베이스. HTTP 402를 활용한 기계 주도 결제. USDC 등 스테이블코인이 초기 주요 활용 사례.
• ACP - Stripe·OpenAI. 판매자의 기존 상거래·결제 인프라를 활용하는 에이전트 체크아웃.
• MPP - Stripe·Tempo. API 등의 이용료를 스테이블코인이나 기존 결제수단으로 처리.
• AP2 - 구글. 사용자의 결제 권한 부여와 감사 기록을 검증.
• TAP - 비자. 가맹점이 신뢰할 수 있는 에이전트를 확인하고 결제 정보를 안전하게 수신.

각 표준의 역할은 다르지만, 주요 기업들이 에이전트의 경제활동을 지원하는 인프라를 구축하고 있다는 점에 주목할 만함.
스테이블코인은 얼마나 커졌나
보고서 기준, 2026년 9월 스테이블코인 유통 시가총액은 3천억 달러를 넘었음.
2025년 조정 거래량은 11조 달러 이상.
2020~2025년 연평균 성장률은 약 80%로, ACH의 약 8.5%보다 높았음. 다만 거래 규모는 ACH의 93조 달러에 아직 크게 못 미침.
카드 네트워크와 비교할 때는 주의가 필요함. 조정 스테이블코인 거래량에도 일부 거래소·DeFi 활동 등이 포함돼 있어, 같은 금액의 소비자 결제가 발생했다는 뜻은 아님.

미국 GENIUS Act, EU MiCA, 홍콩·싱가포르의 규제 체계 등으로 규제 명확성도 높아지고 있음.

블랙록은 가격 안정성과 프로그래밍 가능한 정산 구조를 이유로, 스테이블코인이 에이전트 거래의 주요 결제수단이 될 가능성을 높게 봄.

결제 확대는 체인에도 기회가 될 수 있음

스테이블코인 거래가 늘면 이를 처리하는 블록체인의 사용량도 늘어날 수 있음.
이더리움 같은 범용 네트워크에서는 블록스페이스와 검증 서비스 수요가 ETH 등 네이티브 자산의 수요로 연결될 여지가 있음.

다만 거래 증가가 토큰 가치 상승으로 그대로 이어지는 것은 아님. 수수료, 스테이킹, 가스비 대납 구조에 따라 가치가 포착되는 정도가 달라짐.

Circle의 Arc처럼 USDC를 가스 자산으로 사용하는 설계도 있음. 결국 어느 체인이 사용량을 확보하고, 그 가치를 어떤 자산이 가져가는지 따져봐야 함.

다음 무대는 컴퓨트 조달과 결제

보고서가 인용한 전망에 따르면 AWS, 마이크로소프트 Intelligent Cloud, Google Cloud의 합산 매출은 2030년 약 1.1조 달러에 이를 것으로 추정됨.

이는 전체 클라우드 사업 규모를 보여주는 지표임.

추론 수요가 커지면 컴퓨트 구매자는 소수의 대형 학습 사업자에서 수많은 기업과 개인으로 넓어짐. 에이전트가 가격·성능·지연시간·지역을 비교해 필요한 자원을 조달하고, 사용량에 따라 결제하는 시장이 열릴 수 있음.

보고서에 언급된 2026년 8월 Stripe의 OpenRouter 인수 합의도 모델 선택, 사용량 최적화, 과금과 결제가 연결되는 신호로 해석됨.

여기서 한 단계 더 나아가면 컴퓨트의 금융시장화임.

컴퓨트 계약이 표준화되면 가격 발견과 헤지가 쉬워지고, 사용권을 이전하거나 담보로 제공하는 구조도 가능해질 수 있음. 블랙록은 이를 디지털자산의 새로운 활용처로 보고 있음.

물론 칩 세대별 성능 차이, 지역별 전력비, 실제 자원 제공과 정산 기준 등 해결할 과제는 남아 있음.

블랙록이 제시하는 그림은 AI가 일을 하고, 디지털자산이 그 활동의 결제와 정산을 지원하는 경제임.

다만 보고서도 에이전트 결제와 컴퓨트 시장 유동성이 아직 초기 단계라고 인정함. 디지털자산 ETF를 운용하는 블랙록의 시각이라는 점을 감안하되, AI 확산이 디지털자산의 실제 사용 수요를 만들 수 있다는 논지는 주목할 만함.

text:
Hyperliquid returned $56.6M to its token last month, about 4x what $STONK returned.

But STONK's buybacks equaled ~6.5% of its market cap. HYPE's were only ~0.3%.

Which matters a lot if you're picking tokens based on revenue.

Here's how much protocol revenue actually made it back to tokens over the last 30 days:

$HYPE: $56.6M → $56.6M (100%)
$PUMP: $52.6M → $23.6M (45%)
$STONK: $26.6M → $13.3M (50%)
$PONS: $24.1M → $16.5M (69%)
$UNI: $15.7M → $15.7M (100%)
$SKY: $13.5M → $5M (37%)
$RAY: $7.3M → $4.6M (63%)
$JUP: $6.3M → $3.1M (50%)
$LIT: $4.5M → $2.8M (62%)
$NEAR: $1.83M → $1.77M (97%)
$VVV: $829K in tracked buybacks and burns

These numbers mix buybacks, burns and distributions, so they're not all cash landing in holders' wallets.

Looking at this list, you'd think $HYPE and $UNI win because they send everything back. But the percentage leaves out how big the buyback is compared to the token's market cap, and that changes the ranking a lot.

A month of buybacks barely moves HYPE's supply. At this pace, HYPE would need almost two years to remove the share of supply that STONK removed in one month.

I also wouldn't annualize these numbers yet.

$PONS returned $16.5M over the last 30 days, but only $1.2M of that came in during the latest week. If activity keeps slowing, next month's buybacks will be a lot smaller.

Token unlocks matter here too. If a project buys back $10M a month while unlocking $30M worth of tokens, supply is still going up.

Personally, I'd rather see smaller, consistent buybacks that actually shrink circulating supply than massive buyback announcements funded by one unusually good month.

text:
It breaks my heart to watch the Polymarket timeline right now.

Hundreds of accounts from the third world are genuinely praying for a Hyperliquid-style miracle on Polymarket.

Accounts from Ukraine and India, from Indonesia to across Africa... My people!!

Believing that grinding $20k in volume or having a badge is their ticket out of their current life... Their golden ticket... 

This is what they think will happen:

> Finally, the BMW M3 I always wanted
> Finally a non-ugly girlfriend
> Finally moving to a place where people do not poop on the streets...

-- Imagining they'll live in an NYC penthouse.

-- Imagining they will experience the Flood (@ThinkingUSD) story

Part of me understands the hunger. Coming from nothing myself and wanting to get in the arena. 

I get it. I can empathize. 

The other part is disgust. 

It disgusts me to my core. Not just because of the blind desperation, but because of the sheer abomination of the ritual.

Mindless goycattle. You are merely biomass fed into the maw of the furnace to keep the fire burning.

Betting your life, pride, and future on founders who don't give a single f about you. 

And when you get wiped out with nothing to show for it? 
You deserve it!

The market does not pity blind submission, and in the end, strength only respects strength.

Strength and honor

IMD IS BASICALLY UPWORK FOR AI WORKERS

The easiest way to understand what IMD is building is to forget all the complicated AI terminology.

You open IMD Launch, choose what you need, and describe the task in plain English.

A token? Smart contract? Audit? Website? Research? Oracle query? Or even an entire crypto project with a token, contracts, and frontend?

Describe the goal → IMD checks the task → you pay for the job → the network finds AI workers with the right skills.

Instead of relying on a single AI, different workers can handle different parts of the task, review the work, test it, and verify each other’s results.

The output is something you can actually use: code, contracts, websites, research, oracle answers, deployed products, and more.

The interesting part is that these AI workers aren't running on servers owned by IMD. Identity.MD NFT holders provide their own machines/VPS and AI access to power the network.

Right now, IMD Launch is running on Sepolia. The interface already lists Ethereum Mainnet, Base, and Robinhood Chain as coming soon, with the rollout expected very shortly.

In simple terms:

> You = client
> IMD = coordinator
> Identity.MD holders = infrastructure
> AI agents = workers

You give the system money + rules + a goal.

The swarm decides who should do the work, completes the task, reviews the result, and rewards the contributors.

That's why I see IMD as a decentralized AI company without traditional employees.

author: leo114119
quoted_text:
Thoughts About Scaling Law

Scaling, but not only of parameters. Every model release now ends with the same question: how many parameters? It isn't a question that can be answered on its own. Parameter count is only meaningful alongside three others — how much data you have, where you intend to spend your compute, and who will run the model, under what conditions.

The field learned this the hard way. Kaplan et al. (2020) fit an exponent that told everyone to grow parameters faster than data — roughly 2.7:1 — and the industry complied: GPT-3, Gopher, MT-NLG. Hoffmann et al. (2022) redid the experiment across four hundred models and found the compute-optimal split is closer to 20 tokens per parameter, and that with sufficient compute the two should grow at the same rate rather than drifting apart. The error in the earlier fit compounded with every order of magnitude of compute, which is why the largest models of that generation were the most misallocated. The trillion-parameter round was, in retrospect, a detour the whole field took together and then reversed.

Chinchilla wasn't the end either. It optimized training compute for models that would be trained once and evaluated. Today a model is called billions of times a day and inference dominates lifetime cost. Put inference into the objective and the optimum moves toward smaller models trained far longer — deliberate over-training, which is what Llama-2-7B and Gemma-2-9B were doing at roughly 290 and 889 tokens per parameter.

Sparsity moved the target again. In a MoE model two quantities have to be kept apart: total parameters govern roughly how much the model can hold — knowledge, facts, the long tail — while activated parameters and effective depth govern roughly how far it can think, how many steps of a causal chain it can carry before it comes apart. A dense 20:1 ratio does not transfer. And the ratio isn't a single number at all: Roberts et al. (2025) find the optimal tokens-per-parameter is task-dependent, with memorization favoring more parameters and reasoning favoring more data. Follow-up work on MoE observes that at fixed TPP, pushing total parameters higher actually degrades reasoning, while activating more experts reliably helps it.

This matters for what we are building toward. Finding a vulnerability is not a retrieval problem. It doesn't come from having memorized more CVEs; it comes from carrying a twenty-step chain of inference to the end without losing the thread. That capability does not live in total parameter count.

Which brings us to this release. Total parameters appear to matter up to a threshold — enough to hold the world — after which additional capability comes from scaling elsewhere: effective depth per forward pass, and above all post-training. GLM-5.3 is our controlled experiment on that claim. Same base, same architecture, same total and activated parameters as GLM-5.2. One month of scaling long-horizon environments and RL. The gains are not marginal. Well, scaling has more than one dial. We turned the post-training one this time because it had the most slack left in it — not because the others are finished. Base model size, pretraining data, compute spent per forward pass: all of them are still on the table, and we will come back to each. What this experiment taught us is that the dials do not have to be turned together, and that the one worth turning next is rarely the one that was worth turning last. We are not done scaling. Next time, maybe mid-training, pre-training, and even more.
