quoted_text:
我记得半年前我说自己不怎么 Review PR 了，评论区很多人不认同，觉得这样不靠谱。现在再看，不 Review PR 的人越来越多。比如我刚看的这期播客，在 SpaceXAI 做 Grok Bot 的 Lauren Tan，一个月合并 2500 个 PR，也是不逐个 Review 的：晚上让 AI 自己检查、自己合并，第二天早上她再抽查。

不 Review 不等于不管质量，她靠另外两个办法来保证：
一是让 AI 能像真人用户一样把程序用一遍，自己发现问题；
二是给代码定下很多规矩，让 AI 很难写出烂代码。

她把自己这套做法写成了一组 Skill，公开了出来，叫 pstack。

顺便说一下，这期播客的主持人 Matt Pocock 原本是知名的编程课讲师，他公开的技能库在代码托管网站 GitHub 上有二十多万个星标，是最受欢迎的技能库之一，所以这期算是两位同行对谈。Lauren 之前在 Meta 做网页开发框架 React，今年 3 月加入 AI 编程工具公司 Cursor；Cursor 今年 8 月被 SpaceX 收购，并入旗下的 AI 部门 SpaceXAI。

根据播客的内容，我把 Lauren 的这套做法简单总结一下，我自己的点评在结尾处。

一、先让 AI 能检查自己干的活

Lauren 说，就算不用她的 pstack，每个人最该有的一项技能也是“验证”：给 AI “手和眼睛”，让它能把自己写的程序跑起来，像普通用户一样点一遍，看看结果对不对。

这是她吃过亏之后得出的结论。今年 4 月她在 Cursor 解决一个窗口卡顿的问题，一开始全靠手工：她自己去看各种性能数据，再把看到的转述给 AI，AI 改完她再去看。她形容自己成了 AI 和检测工具之间的“人肉中转站”。她在 Cursor 写的第一个技能就是验证。在这之前，AI 看不到自己改动的效果，只能等她来回传话；有了验证，AI 可以自己改、自己看结果、不满意再改，一轮一轮往下做，不需要她守着。现在她所在的团队里每个产品都配有这样的验证技能，全团队都在用。

做这个技能时她还总结出一条原则：工作里有的部分需要动脑判断，有的部分只是照章办事，照章办事的部分应该写成固定的程序，只把需要判断的留给 AI。起因是她发现，每个 AI 在检查前都要自己从头写一遍检查用的小程序，各写各的，有的能用有的不能用，用完就扔，又慢又浪费。她把这部分做成一个现成的工具，所有 AI 直接调用。

二、AI 反复犯的错，去改规矩，不去改 AI

Lauren 不喜欢“软件工厂”这个流行说法，她更愿意把自己的工作比作经营一家米其林餐厅的后厨。主厨不用亲手做每道菜，但要安排好整个厨房：食材什么时候进、怎么存，每个人用什么工具，菜按什么流程出。工程师现在也一样，不再亲手写代码，却仍然要对结果负责。她认为工程师现在最重要的工作就是把这个“厨房”布置好。没花时间布置的人，信不过 AI 的产出，只能盯着它一步步干，忙到没空改进工具，就像一直拿钝刀切菜。

她举了自己的例子。Grok Bot 最早几版的代码挤在八个巨大的文件里，每个至少一万行，AI 加新功能时就接着往里塞，越塞越乱。她后来定了规矩：每个功能必须放在自己单独的文件夹里，做一件事只允许一种写法，不合规矩的代码会被自动检查拦下来。这样 AI 加功能时不用多想，按规矩放就行。她的习惯是一直观察 AI 在哪里出错，每看到一次就问自己：能不能加一条规矩，让这种错以后根本写不出来。

不逐个检查，靠的也是这套办法。她说，开了几家餐厅的老板不可能尝每一道菜，只能抽查。她每天挑一些改动仔细看，如果只是偶然出错就算了；如果好几个 AI 都在走同一条捷径，说明该改的是规矩和工具。她的 pstack 里有一个全自动模式：每次改动都会派出一批专门负责检查的 AI，把程序打开到处点，找出问题就自己修，反复到没问题再合并。早上她翻一遍改动记录，发现不对就撤回，再补一条新规矩。

她说第一次让 AI 整夜自己合并代码时很害怕，担心半夜把线上产品弄坏，现在反而睡得更好。她也提醒，走到这一步很难，要花大量时间观察和调整，装上 pstack 并不能直接做到。Matt 问，如果改动是没法撤回的，比如会丢数据，或者是医疗、金融这类领域怎么办？她说这取决于工作成果能不能被程序自动检查，软件大部分可以，很难自动检查的领域就很难这样做，她自己也没有答案。

三、2500 次改动从哪来：她不再当传话的人

这 2500 次改动并不是她发起了 2500 次对话。用户反馈的问题散落在聊天工具、邮件和社交媒体上，以前要靠她自己去看，再转述给 AI。现在她让 Grok Bot 来盯这些渠道。Grok Bot 是 SpaceXAI 今年 8 月推出的产品，是能登录邮箱、聊天工具等各种应用、替人办事的 AI 智能体。它一发现新的问题反馈，就转给一个负责“协调”的 AI。这个协调者自己不写代码，只负责拆分任务、分派给其他 AI、盯进度，相当于她的后厨主管。

为什么不直接一个问题派一个 AI 去修？她说，一批反馈往往出自同一个根源，分开修会重复劳动，也看不出真正的毛病在哪，放在一起看才看得出来。她现在同时开着十多个这样的协调者，各管一摊。她一直在问自己一个问题：哪一步还卡在我身上，AI 为什么非得来问我？然后想办法教 AI 自己去拿到真实的信息。

她也说明，2500 次改动里新功能不占多数，很多是整理代码这类维护工作。

四、懂行的人更吃香，哪怕不会写代码

Matt 问，大家都靠 AI 了，专业知识是不是不值钱了？Lauren 的看法相反。模型越来越强，卡住人的已经变成你能不能把自己想要什么讲清楚。所以她认为，医生、律师这类在某个领域懂得很深的人，只要稍微懂一点技术、会用 AI 智能体，就能做出很好的产品。

两人都认为，技能没有什么神秘的，就是把自己的做事流程写成文字。Lauren 建议回头翻自己和 AI 的聊天记录，找出那些自己反复纠正、反复插手的地方，把它们写成技能或规矩。别人的技能可以拿来拼着用，但每个人最后都该有一套自己的，就像厨师换了餐厅也会带着自己的刀。

五、最后

很多人看完这期访谈会觉得，以后自己也可以像 Lauren 那样不 Review PR 了，装上她的 Skill，让模型帮忙验证一下就行。我自己现在的做法和她差不多，每天也有大量 PR，也不 Review。但我的建议是先别急着学她怎么做，先弄明白她凭什么能这么做。

1. 你能不能用上最好的模型，Token 够不够

在用上 Fable 和 Opus 5.5 之前，AI 写的代码我是不太放心的；用上之后，我才真的敢让 AI 去写而不怎么 Review。模型能力很重要，能力没到，就先别想这件事。

还有成本。像我这样没有大公司可以依靠的，得自己掏钱买 2 个 Claude Max 20x 账号，还得省着用。Lauren 在大公司，不用考虑 Token 消耗，全程用最好的模型、开最快的模式都没问题。

不过也别着急。Fable 这个级别的模型，也许半年以后就能像现在的 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 一样便宜，人人用得起。梁圣加油。

2. 不能完全依赖 AI 的验证

哪怕现在 GPT-6 操作电脑的水平已经超过真人了，让它去做验证，也只能替代一部分，不能真的全交给它，自己还是要看。

可以做的是把那些手动重复做的事情，一点点沉淀成 Skill 和自动化脚本，把体力活解放出去。

3. 方向得靠你自己的专业来指

再聪明的 AI，也没办法替你决定该往哪个方向走。就像给车子装上火箭发动机，也得你来告诉它往哪开，走偏了要及时调整，不然跑得再快也是南辕北辙。

做软件也一样。你不能指望一句提示词做出一个淘宝。你得先做一个能发商品、能浏览的小网站，再加上用户注册，还得区分买家和卖家，然后是支付和安全，功能做完了还要扛得住很多人同时用。稍微复杂一点的软件，都没法完全依赖 AI，要人去拆解、规划，分成一个个小版本、小里程碑，做完要验证，出现偏差要重新指方向。甚至做着做着，你自己的想法都变了，AI 不可能知道你真正想要的是什么。

所以就像播客里说的：模型越来越强，卡住人的已经变成你能不能把自己想要什么讲清楚。

4. 不一定要用他们的 Skill，但要学着把事情交给 Agent 去做

Matt 和 Lauren 的 Skill 都很受欢迎，但你不一定要用。

一方面，软件工程的基础知识，现在的模型已经学得很好了。Lauren 在播客里也说，去年的 Skill 还得写清楚具体该敲哪条命令，现在这些都可以删掉，只留流程步骤，Skill 会越写越短。

另一方面，他们的开发流程和环境，跟你的很可能不一样。Lauren 的 Skill 都是从她自己的工作里总结出来的：验证技能来自她当“人肉中转站”的那段日子；另一个叫 recall 的技能，来自她每次开新对话，都得把上一个对话里的背景再讲一遍。

所以更重要的是从你自己每天的开发流程出发。那些还要你手动操作的环节，尽可能交给 Agent 去做；Agent 做顺了，再把它的操作过程沉淀成 Skill，反复迭代优化。

如果不知道从哪里下手的话，可以参考 Lauren 的办法：翻自己和 AI 的聊天记录，找那些你反复纠正、反复插手的地方。这样迭代出来的 Skill 才真正适合你，用她的话说，每个厨师都该有一套自己的刀。

text:
We’re already starting to see what kind of new jobs AI is creating. 

AI requires significant technical work and surrounding services to deploy into the economy. This means jobs for AI engineers that build applied AI products sold to (or within) enterprises, FDEs to deploy agents into companies, new services firms for deploying AI, and more. 

And even the published stats of new jobs undercount all the existing jobs that are transitioning to new areas of AI work in an enterprise. Many prior data, research, and software jobs large enterprises are also being repositioned for working with AI. 

Every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and even law firm is bringing on more technical talent -or repositioning existing roles- to help with agent deployment in their companies. It’s a lot easier to picture what AI can replace vs. what it creates until it starts happening. Now we’re seeing what this looks like.
author: levie
quoted_text:
AI-related employment is surging:

AI-linked roles have accounted for more than +750,000 new jobs created in the US since 2023, according to LinkedIn estimates.

This surge has been led by data annotators, with +282,000 new positions created, followed by data center jobs at +117,000, and AI engineers at +105,000.

As a result, these 3 categories have accounted for +504,000 new jobs.

AI-related positions also offer significantly higher pay, with a median salary of ~$180,000 on LinkedIn, compared to $80,000 across all jobs.

This comes as the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, particularly the buildout of data centers, is driving stronger demand for labor.

The AI boom is reshaping the US job market.

text:
When HDHPs started to become a "thing", I thought they may be the best things since sliced bread.... for about an hour (or less).  

An HDHP sounds good at face value - a triple tax savings vehicle.  Maybe - for a chosen few.  

First, the premiums for a HDHP aren't really that much lower than other plans.

Second, if you pay for an HDHP, you also get the honor of paying the first $2000, $3000, etc. of your healthcare expenses.  I just talked to a group last week.  When I asked what their premium was, they said "$456 for single".  I told them that it could be better but it wasn't the worse I'd seen and then ask what the individual deductible was.  $9000!!!  

That isn't a plan, that is theft by deception.  These people are paying over $5000 per year so that they can pay $9000 per year if they need healthcare.  Total - $14K per year before those billions dollar insurance companies PAY A DIME!  That's $1166/month if major medical is needed.  That's groceries for a month - life sustaining food not "just in case I have a heart attack" money. 

So, THEN you get to delays, denials, etc.  Imagine paying $14K for coverage for life saving medical needs to be denied.  That is what happens.

40% of health plans in the U.S. are ERISA plans - State insurance laws don't really apply so State Insurance Commissioners are off the hook for those.  

Then you get to the word "law".  Sadly, "law" applies to those chosen by the government for it to apply to.  Laws are written but not enforced.  The Transparency Act has been in effect for over 5 years.  It's just paper.  An Executive Order was signed to enforce that law.  It's just paper.

Then you get to our ever faithful IRS - non-profit hospitals are holding BILLIONS in "profit", buying up real estate every second of every day - real estate that they pay ZERO real estate taxes on causing the real estate taxes of average  Americans to skyrocket AND, since the real estate is owned by the hospital, they get to charge you for the luxury of walking through the friggin' door to see your doctor, who they also own, so they can overcharge you again.... meanwhile, in the C-Suites, CEOs are making tens of millions in salaries, flying on chartered plains, joining social clubs (hospitals pay the dues), etc.  Does the IRS care?  No.  When is the last time a non-profit was audited.  Now ask "when is the last time the IRS audited a normal business man?"  Daily.  Hourly.  

Lest we not forget, our government mandates that employers with over 50 employees cover their employees and the government mandates what must be covered (aka - they have to pay for coverage for their employees that may not be coverage at all when needed).  Employers can give their employees money to buy coverage BUT, that money must be used to buy coverage on an individual basis.  They can't just bank it and use it for medical expenses.  By law, they MUST purchase what is called "insurance" from the same corrupt organizations that were sell it to employers.

Then lets get to the $1M claim.  I've seen dozens of $1M claims in 30 years.  Never have I seen one that was actually payable at $1M.  Hospitals inflate charges, they unbundle charges and they simply make up charges.  But still, a claim should be paid, no matter what the amount, when medically necessary.

To Mark's point - the entire healthcare industry (with the few exceptions of independent physicians, labs, imaging, etc) IS compromised.

And finally, if you are looking at a health insurance product, period, BE CAREFUL - it is likely rigged against you.  

Do not, under any circumstance, believe that any form of government is coming to save you from healthcare costs.  We are on our own.  

As a side note, our government, with its last CAA, made being the fiduciary over a health plan more burdensome on company CEOs, owners, etc. so not only does the government look the other way, they put the burden of overseeing the health plans on YOU, the employer and that burden is immense.

quoted_text:
So I went down the rabbit hole of trying to determine what are the economics for someone, who is currently healthy , to go to a HDHP with a 10k plus deductible.  

The question I asked is “I dont trust insurance companies. What happens if I have a million dollar emergency and they won’t pay “.  All I can say is WTF 

If they don’t pay, there are Independent Review Organizations, who are supposed to be independent, and their decision to pay or not is final.   I asked for examples of companies. One was ExamWorks.  That rang a bell.   

These motherfuckers are the same company that issued a ridiculous denial for a patient I was trying to help.   So I knew the Too Big To Care, vertically integrated insurance companies hired them to do DENIALS !!! WTF.  

The biggest customers of the companies that are the final decision makers for insurance carrier denials, are the biggest insurance companies. 

That is beyond fucked up.  It’s the definition of conflict of interest.   How do state insurance commissioners allow this ?

The  high deductible plans that many people say is the solution to fixing how we do insurance,  may be effectively compromised 

If you are looking at a HDHP, BE CAREFUL 

It might just be rigged against you

author: benitoz
quoted_text:
AI Drug Discovery Is Becoming a Bottleneck Trade

I get excited when an industry starts going through a real regime change. AI drug discovery (“AIDD”) increasingly looks like one of those moments.

Two things are happening:
1/ Upstream: the frontier AI labs are piling in.
2/ Downstream: The supply chain is clearly moving.

Supply-chain checks suggest the upstream picks-and-shovels of discovery and early preclinical R&D are starting to feel the increase in experimental volume.

DNA → protein → assays → sequencing → automation → preclinical testing

Names across that stack include $TWST , @GenScript , $ILMN , $TXG , lab-automation vendors and CROs.

$TWST expects triple-digit percentage growth in AI-enabled drug-discovery orders in FY26, and another year of triple-digit order growth in FY27.

@GenScript's AIDD business doubled YoY in 1H26. Its current platform advertises industrial-scale validation of 4,000+ designs/day, with integrated sequence-to-data workflows. Our channel checks suggest the ramp is moving even faster: roughly 8,000 designs/day currently, with a path toward ~16,000/day by YE26.

---
Why does AI drive more wet-lab demand?

1/ AI makes hypothesis generation almost free → way more shots on goal.
The bottleneck is moving from expert-driven design to biological validation.

2/ AI models need continuous experimental feedback — and both good and bad data are useful.
Traditionally, only the highest-conviction A+ candidates might get pushed into expensive validation. With AI, even the B/C candidates can be valuable because failed experiments generate training data.

@GenScript has said its sequence-to-binding workflow can return data in 4–7 days, and that faster cycle times matter because AI models depend on continuous experimental feedback.

@Anthropic is a clean example. @claudeai  designed 1,320 protein binders. @adaptyvbio  converted those digital sequences into DNA, expressed the proteins and tested binding. Only 354 actually bound. And the 966 failures are not wasted. They are useful negative labels: what does not express, what does not bind, what has poor affinity. Those results help train the next model iteration.

3/ Wet labs are no longer just making drugs. They are making training data.
$TWST  / @GenScript  increasingly look like biological data foundries.

$TWST explicitly talks about generating model-ready data from AI-designed sequences. In some workflows, the customer may care less about receiving the physical protein than about getting structured experimental results back into the model.

Traditional drug discovery asks: “Does candidate X work?”

AI drug discovery also asks: “What can this experiment teach the model?”

---
TAM of AIDD

If AI is simply a better R&D tool, the relevant spending pool is the $300–400B of annual global pharma R&D. If AI meaningfully increases the number of viable drug programs, the opportunity is larger because it expands downstream demand for DNA synthesis, protein production, assays, and preclinical work.

Near term, we can also size demand from AI-company spending. If Anthropic reaches $80B of ARR in 2026 and spends just 1% on AIDD, that alone would imply ~$800M of annual investment.

---
Trade setup

This is a trade that could have long legs. It’s hard to really stop working until PhaseI/II results (2028+)

It smells a lot like the bottleneck trade we just saw in semis: GPUs → HBM → networking → power/cooling. In biology, It basically follows the drug discovery process downstream: AI models → designs → DNA/protein → assays → preclinical capacity.

After the upstream picks-and-shovels, animal testing could become the next bottleneck. Monkey prices are already near prior highs and CRO capacity is tight. AIDD pushing more candidates into preclinical development would only add demand.

?? But clinical trials are still the bottleneck?
This is the biggest pushback I keep coming back to. No matter how fast discovery becomes, drugs still need to go through preclinical → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III → approval. You still need patients, time and capital.

But that doesn’t mean the bottleneck trade won’t work. More viable candidates — especially with higher success rates — still means more demand throughout the development process.

And who knows: clinical trials themselves may eventually be optimized by AI.

?? What breaks the trade?
Near term, the picks-and-shovels trade breaks if experimental budgets stop growing, AI-generated designs don’t translate into useful wet-lab hits, or capacity catches up too quickly.

Longer term, the thesis breaks if AI drugs look great in discovery / Phase I but fail at normal rates in Phase II/III. That is why Phase II matters so much.

?? Milestones
Late 2026–2027: first Isomorphic-designed drugs enter human trials; more AI-native programs move into IND-enabling work / tox.

2028–2030: clinical trial results start telling us whether AI-designed drugs actually perform better than conventional drugs.

Calling all the "bottleneck bros". :) @jukan05 @zephyr_z9 @aleabitoreddit @ParadisLabs 

+++
More comprehensive analysis: https://t.co/vaTuiyyYB6

text:
我记得半年前我说自己不怎么 Review PR 了，评论区很多人不认同，觉得这样不靠谱。现在再看，不 Review PR 的人越来越多。比如我刚看的这期播客，在 SpaceXAI 做 Grok Bot 的 Lauren Tan，一个月合并 2500 个 PR，也是不逐个 Review 的：晚上让 AI 自己检查、自己合并，第二天早上她再抽查。

不 Review 不等于不管质量，她靠另外两个办法来保证：
一是让 AI 能像真人用户一样把程序用一遍，自己发现问题；
二是给代码定下很多规矩，让 AI 很难写出烂代码。

她把自己这套做法写成了一组 Skill，公开了出来，叫 pstack。

顺便说一下，这期播客的主持人 Matt Pocock 原本是知名的编程课讲师，他公开的技能库在代码托管网站 GitHub 上有二十多万个星标，是最受欢迎的技能库之一，所以这期算是两位同行对谈。Lauren 之前在 Meta 做网页开发框架 React，今年 3 月加入 AI 编程工具公司 Cursor；Cursor 今年 8 月被 SpaceX 收购，并入旗下的 AI 部门 SpaceXAI。

根据播客的内容，我把 Lauren 的这套做法简单总结一下，我自己的点评在结尾处。

一、先让 AI 能检查自己干的活

Lauren 说，就算不用她的 pstack，每个人最该有的一项技能也是“验证”：给 AI “手和眼睛”，让它能把自己写的程序跑起来，像普通用户一样点一遍，看看结果对不对。

这是她吃过亏之后得出的结论。今年 4 月她在 Cursor 解决一个窗口卡顿的问题，一开始全靠手工：她自己去看各种性能数据，再把看到的转述给 AI，AI 改完她再去看。她形容自己成了 AI 和检测工具之间的“人肉中转站”。她在 Cursor 写的第一个技能就是验证。在这之前，AI 看不到自己改动的效果，只能等她来回传话；有了验证，AI 可以自己改、自己看结果、不满意再改，一轮一轮往下做，不需要她守着。现在她所在的团队里每个产品都配有这样的验证技能，全团队都在用。

做这个技能时她还总结出一条原则：工作里有的部分需要动脑判断，有的部分只是照章办事，照章办事的部分应该写成固定的程序，只把需要判断的留给 AI。起因是她发现，每个 AI 在检查前都要自己从头写一遍检查用的小程序，各写各的，有的能用有的不能用，用完就扔，又慢又浪费。她把这部分做成一个现成的工具，所有 AI 直接调用。

二、AI 反复犯的错，去改规矩，不去改 AI

Lauren 不喜欢“软件工厂”这个流行说法，她更愿意把自己的工作比作经营一家米其林餐厅的后厨。主厨不用亲手做每道菜，但要安排好整个厨房：食材什么时候进、怎么存，每个人用什么工具，菜按什么流程出。工程师现在也一样，不再亲手写代码，却仍然要对结果负责。她认为工程师现在最重要的工作就是把这个“厨房”布置好。没花时间布置的人，信不过 AI 的产出，只能盯着它一步步干，忙到没空改进工具，就像一直拿钝刀切菜。

她举了自己的例子。Grok Bot 最早几版的代码挤在八个巨大的文件里，每个至少一万行，AI 加新功能时就接着往里塞，越塞越乱。她后来定了规矩：每个功能必须放在自己单独的文件夹里，做一件事只允许一种写法，不合规矩的代码会被自动检查拦下来。这样 AI 加功能时不用多想，按规矩放就行。她的习惯是一直观察 AI 在哪里出错，每看到一次就问自己：能不能加一条规矩，让这种错以后根本写不出来。

不逐个检查，靠的也是这套办法。她说，开了几家餐厅的老板不可能尝每一道菜，只能抽查。她每天挑一些改动仔细看，如果只是偶然出错就算了；如果好几个 AI 都在走同一条捷径，说明该改的是规矩和工具。她的 pstack 里有一个全自动模式：每次改动都会派出一批专门负责检查的 AI，把程序打开到处点，找出问题就自己修，反复到没问题再合并。早上她翻一遍改动记录，发现不对就撤回，再补一条新规矩。

她说第一次让 AI 整夜自己合并代码时很害怕，担心半夜把线上产品弄坏，现在反而睡得更好。她也提醒，走到这一步很难，要花大量时间观察和调整，装上 pstack 并不能直接做到。Matt 问，如果改动是没法撤回的，比如会丢数据，或者是医疗、金融这类领域怎么办？她说这取决于工作成果能不能被程序自动检查，软件大部分可以，很难自动检查的领域就很难这样做，她自己也没有答案。

三、2500 次改动从哪来：她不再当传话的人

这 2500 次改动并不是她发起了 2500 次对话。用户反馈的问题散落在聊天工具、邮件和社交媒体上，以前要靠她自己去看，再转述给 AI。现在她让 Grok Bot 来盯这些渠道。Grok Bot 是 SpaceXAI 今年 8 月推出的产品，是能登录邮箱、聊天工具等各种应用、替人办事的 AI 智能体。它一发现新的问题反馈，就转给一个负责“协调”的 AI。这个协调者自己不写代码，只负责拆分任务、分派给其他 AI、盯进度，相当于她的后厨主管。

为什么不直接一个问题派一个 AI 去修？她说，一批反馈往往出自同一个根源，分开修会重复劳动，也看不出真正的毛病在哪，放在一起看才看得出来。她现在同时开着十多个这样的协调者，各管一摊。她一直在问自己一个问题：哪一步还卡在我身上，AI 为什么非得来问我？然后想办法教 AI 自己去拿到真实的信息。

她也说明，2500 次改动里新功能不占多数，很多是整理代码这类维护工作。

四、懂行的人更吃香，哪怕不会写代码

Matt 问，大家都靠 AI 了，专业知识是不是不值钱了？Lauren 的看法相反。模型越来越强，卡住人的已经变成你能不能把自己想要什么讲清楚。所以她认为，医生、律师这类在某个领域懂得很深的人，只要稍微懂一点技术、会用 AI 智能体，就能做出很好的产品。

两人都认为，技能没有什么神秘的，就是把自己的做事流程写成文字。Lauren 建议回头翻自己和 AI 的聊天记录，找出那些自己反复纠正、反复插手的地方，把它们写成技能或规矩。别人的技能可以拿来拼着用，但每个人最后都该有一套自己的，就像厨师换了餐厅也会带着自己的刀。

五、最后

很多人看完这期访谈会觉得，以后自己也可以像 Lauren 那样不 Review PR 了，装上她的 Skill，让模型帮忙验证一下就行。我自己现在的做法和她差不多，每天也有大量 PR，也不 Review。但我的建议是先别急着学她怎么做，先弄明白她凭什么能这么做。

1. 你能不能用上最好的模型，Token 够不够

在用上 Fable 和 Opus 5.5 之前，AI 写的代码我是不太放心的；用上之后，我才真的敢让 AI 去写而不怎么 Review。模型能力很重要，能力没到，就先别想这件事。

还有成本。像我这样没有大公司可以依靠的，得自己掏钱买 2 个 Claude Max 20x 账号，还得省着用。Lauren 在大公司，不用考虑 Token 消耗，全程用最好的模型、开最快的模式都没问题。

不过也别着急。Fable 这个级别的模型，也许半年以后就能像现在的 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 一样便宜，人人用得起。梁圣加油。

2. 不能完全依赖 AI 的验证

哪怕现在 GPT-6 操作电脑的水平已经超过真人了，让它去做验证，也只能替代一部分，不能真的全交给它，自己还是要看。

可以做的是把那些手动重复做的事情，一点点沉淀成 Skill 和自动化脚本，把体力活解放出去。

3. 方向得靠你自己的专业来指

再聪明的 AI，也没办法替你决定该往哪个方向走。就像给车子装上火箭发动机，也得你来告诉它往哪开，走偏了要及时调整，不然跑得再快也是南辕北辙。

做软件也一样。你不能指望一句提示词做出一个淘宝。你得先做一个能发商品、能浏览的小网站，再加上用户注册，还得区分买家和卖家，然后是支付和安全，功能做完了还要扛得住很多人同时用。稍微复杂一点的软件，都没法完全依赖 AI，要人去拆解、规划，分成一个个小版本、小里程碑，做完要验证，出现偏差要重新指方向。甚至做着做着，你自己的想法都变了，AI 不可能知道你真正想要的是什么。

所以就像播客里说的：模型越来越强，卡住人的已经变成你能不能把自己想要什么讲清楚。

4. 不一定要用他们的 Skill，但要学着把事情交给 Agent 去做

Matt 和 Lauren 的 Skill 都很受欢迎，但你不一定要用。

一方面，软件工程的基础知识，现在的模型已经学得很好了。Lauren 在播客里也说，去年的 Skill 还得写清楚具体该敲哪条命令，现在这些都可以删掉，只留流程步骤，Skill 会越写越短。

另一方面，他们的开发流程和环境，跟你的很可能不一样。Lauren 的 Skill 都是从她自己的工作里总结出来的：验证技能来自她当“人肉中转站”的那段日子；另一个叫 recall 的技能，来自她每次开新对话，都得把上一个对话里的背景再讲一遍。

所以更重要的是从你自己每天的开发流程出发。那些还要你手动操作的环节，尽可能交给 Agent 去做；Agent 做顺了，再把它的操作过程沉淀成 Skill，反复迭代优化。

如果不知道从哪里下手的话，可以参考 Lauren 的办法：翻自己和 AI 的聊天记录，找那些你反复纠正、反复插手的地方。这样迭代出来的 Skill 才真正适合你，用她的话说，每个厨师都该有一套自己的刀。

chatgpt recommends them because when someone asks "what should i use for my backend" the entire internet already points to supabase.

but heres what blew my mind:

supabase gets 0 citations on chatgpt for queries about their own core features:

> "how do i make sure each user can only read their own rows in postgres" - this is literally row level security. supabase's signature feature. chatgpt doesnt cite them. doesnt even mention them.

> "how do i push realtime updates to the browser when my database changes" - realtime is one of their 5 core products. 0 citations.

> "how do i add google login and magic links to a next.js app" - supabase auth does exactly this. 0 citations.

> "best vector database for a RAG app" - they shipped pgvector before almost everyone. 0 citations. qdrant and aws get cited instead.

the pattern: supabase wins every query where someone names the category. but when someone describes the job they need done  (the exact problems supabase solves) the AI has no page to link to.

firebase is even wilder. mentioned 15 times across all queries but only cited twice. every AI knows firebase exists. none of them have a reason to link to it.

supabase built one of the greatest developer platforms ever. and even they have blind spots in AI search.

text:
FCC is easiest to understand by looking at where the trust boundary sits. 🔍

In the weather insurance example below, the smart contract keeps policy state and handles payouts, but the sensitive or external work happens inside a TEE.

The smart contract can request work from the confidential compute environment without exposing the sensitive inputs onchain. Inside the TEE, the application can decrypt the private policy terms, pull weather data from OpenWeatherMap, run the rainfall calculation and sign the result.

The contract then verifies that signed result before releasing a payout.

So the chain does not need to execute the private logic or trust an unsigned API response. It only accepts the result produced by the registered confidential compute environment.

The repo includes the Solidity contracts, Go extension, proxy setup, Coston2 deployment scripts and frontend:

text:
Jeff Hinton dismissed gradient descent entirely before winning the Nobel Prize for it. His fear was local minima - valleys in the loss landscape where the model gets stuck forever. For a 1.2 billion parameter LLM like Llama, the landscape has more dimensions than atoms in the observable universe. Getting permanently stuck would require hitting a dead end in every single dimension simultaneously.

What gradient descent actually looks like on a real LLM is stranger than anyone expected. Take two random directions through that billion-dimensional space, visualize the loss surface, and watch what happens when training starts - a wormhole opens and the model drops into a low-loss valley that wasn't visible from the starting point. The valley was always nearby in high-dimensional space. It just couldn't be seen in the 2D projection.

20 minutes. Bookmark & watch today. The most honest visualization of how LLMs actually learn.

text:
Evil is the cheap story. It lets people keep the old map and just draw a demon on it.
What’s being broken is not “good people versus a bad machine.” It’s the operating system civilization ran on. That system is older than any lab. It is the set of assumptions a town, a school, a court, a church, a company, and a family used without naming them. AI does not debate those assumptions. It makes them stop working in practice.
For a long time the world ran on scarcity of the finished thing.
Making a finished page, a finished picture, a finished song, a finished brief, a finished diagnosis sketch, a finished design, a finished excuse — that took time, training, tools, and usually an institution standing behind you. Because it was expensive, most people consumed and a few produced. Because it was expensive, a diploma, a letterhead, a photograph, a voice on a phone, a clip on the news, a signature, a uniform, could be treated as proof. Not perfect proof. Good enough proof. Civilization is not built on perfect proof. It is built on proof that is costly enough that most people will not fake it every day.
Privacy was the default for the same reason. Copying a person was hard. Seeing a body was local. Hearing a voice meant the person was there or the recording was rare. Clothes were not just cloth. They were a lock. Shame was a control system that only works if concealment is scarce and exposure is expensive.
Status came from being the one who could do the rare skill. Institutions were the bottleneck. If you wanted scale, you went through school, studio, paper, pulpit, HR, the union, the state, the label, the board. That was not always fair. It was stable. Stability is what people mean when they say “civilization as we know it.” They do not mean marble columns. They mean the rules of evidence that let a stranger be believed.
AI is not a villain walking into that arrangement. It is a change in the price of copies.
When the copy of a page, a face, a voice, a lesson, a contract, a song, a plan, a confession, a lie, becomes cheap, every system that ran on scarce copies starts to wobble. That is the destruction. It does not look like a crater. It looks like a world that still has buildings, flags, and offices, and no longer agrees on what a document is.
This is why the people building the tool often do not understand what they are doing. They are staring at the arrow. Accuracy. Latency. Benchmarks. Parameters. Alignment. Refusal rates. Monthly users. Whether the model will draw the wrong thing. Whether it will say the wrong thing. Those are craftsman’s questions. They are not civilization questions.
The civilization question is distance.
A bow matters because a smaller person can change a larger thing without standing next to it. Gun, artillery, missile, network, algorithm — same structure, better range, better aim, better payload. AI in this decade is the first reliable way for a single nervous system to act at a distance on language, pictures, sound, code, memory, and paperwork. The payload is still crude. The range is already global. Ten years of “more and better,” used by the old, the average, and the young, does not require a god in a box. It only requires the price of a finished first version to keep falling.
What dies first is not cities. What dies first is proof.
If anyone can write the brief, the brief stops being proof of a lawyer. The lawyer still exists. The paper stops being the sacrament. If anyone can make the song, the recording stops being proof of a band. The live body in the room starts to matter more, not less, because flesh is what the copy cannot be. If anyone can make the picture of a body, clothing and “I didn’t see that” stop being the social contract they were. If anyone can make the voice, the phone call stops being proof it was them. If anyone can make the first version of the code, the company, the lesson, the sermon, the ad, the apology — those institutions keep the letterhead and lose the monopoly.
Gatekeepers get louder while they get weaker. That phase is ugly and it is already here. Schools still talk like they own learning. Companies still talk like they own “professional appearance.” Platforms still talk like they own speech. States still talk like they own the official story. They all still have buildings. The monopoly is what is rotting. When a monopoly rots, it does not go quiet. It passes more rules.
This is the part that looks like “AI will destroy civilization” to people who only have the old map. They are watching the proofs fail and calling it the end of the world. It is the end of this edition. Manuscript culture felt that way when print arrived. Print culture felt that way when the feed arrived. Each time the copy got cheaper, the priesthood of the previous copy called it ruin. Sometimes they were pointing at a real wound. They were still wrong about the shape of the event. The event was not demons. The event was distance.
Trust thins. That is the central social fact of the next ten years, whether anyone likes it or not. You will believe people you already know in the flesh. You will treat the rest of the feed as weather. Courts, schools, hiring, dating, journalism, reputation, “I know what I saw” — all of those ran on a background assumption that a recording was expensive enough to be evidence. When a recording is cheap, evidence has to move. It moves toward presence. Toward a name you can find in a town. Toward work you can hold. Toward a person who will stand there and say it again tomorrow. That is not romance. That is what survives when the copy is free.
Work splits on a different axis than “smart versus dumb.” The split is people who own a loop versus people who wait to be told. A loop is: point the tool, judge the output, put it in the world, take the hit if it is wrong. The old middle — first drafts, summaries, layouts, scheduling, the clean version of a messy thing — gets eaten or shrunk before the culture has a story about what the middle was for. A one-person shop can look like a company. A company can look like a building full of people waiting for a prompt. Wages get weird. Meaning gets weirder. A lot of dignity was stored in being the one who could make the scarce page. When the page is not scarce, dignity has to be stored somewhere else or it evaporates into resentment.
Kids and old people feel the change earlier than labs do. A child with a helper that talks at their pace is not the same child as one parked in front of a mute screen. An old person who can still run a shop because the tool holds the steps is not the same retirement as one that depended on a fading memory and a younger relative who may or may not come. Both can be grace. Both can be a new kind of neglect. The tool does not choose. The household does. Places with power and a signal will treat this as normal. Places without it will treat it as a new poverty: not “no food,” but “no range.”
Power uses the bow. That sentence should not surprise anyone and it surprises people every time. “The people get the tool” is true. “Only the people get the tool” is a children’s story. States will use it to write law, write the reply to your complaint, sort the school, sort the threat, sort the crowd. Companies will use it to write the ad, the review, the performance plan, the denial. Churches and movements will use it to write the sermon and the enemy. Kings used bows. They will use this. The difference is that a lot of ordinary people get a bow too. That is new. It is not the same as the kings putting theirs down.
The body piece belongs here, because it is not a side issue. For a long time civilization used cloth as administration. Cover the body, and you could administer shame, work, gender, age, class, and belonging with a glance. That only holds if the uncovered body is scarce. When anyone can picture a body, concealment stops being a public utility. Two things happen at once, and people who want a single moral keep missing both. More people dress as signal instead of as lock — wear what they mean, because hiding is no longer the point. And more people get pictured as they did not mean. Law will chase the second and mostly miss. Custom will move on the first whether law likes it or not. Ten years is enough for custom to shift. It is not enough for statute to catch it clean. That lag is what a lot of the screaming will be about.
None of this requires an evil superintelligence. It does not require the machine to “wake up” and hate you. It only requires the bow getting better while humans stay human. Humans will use a longer reach for care, craft, sex, spite, worship, laziness, and war, because that is what humans used every longer reach for. The flood of almost-true pictures and voices does not need a villain. People who never learn a craft because the first draft was always good enough do not need a villain. Loneliness sold as a companion that never needs you back does not need a villain. Those are default settings.
The nuke analog is a different object. The nuke analog is when the same stack can reliably design new harms at civilization scale, or run a factory or a war loop with almost no one in it. That is not the same event as “proof got cheap.” People who smash those two together are trying to keep the demon map. People who say they know the month of the nuke are selling. You can see the bow clearly without pretending you can see the yield of a weapon that is not here yet.
What the builders miss, at the deepest level, is that they think they are adding a product to civilization. They are changing what counts as real. A lab can understand gradients and still not understand that they made proof cheap. Once proof is cheap, every system that ran on scarce proof has to be rebuilt or it becomes costume.
The next edition will still have families, work, violence, churches, shops, land, hunger, and people who want to be seen a certain way. It will not run on the same proofs. Meaning will lean back toward things the copy cannot be: a live room, a field, a wound, a child in front of you, a name that has to answer in the morning. That will look, to the old system, like collapse. It is closer to a molt.
Civilization is not ending. This edition is. The people making the tool are measuring the arrow. The event is the moment after distance exists, when the tribe has to relearn what a hunt even is.

An RL setup for training decision models that return calibrated probabilities instead of text.

The input is encoded once, every option runs as its own branch, and a single scorer turns each branch into a probability.

During training, real outcomes are sampled from each item's label, and the model is rewarded on two things: the probability it gave to what actually happened, and whether its confidence in its own decision was honest.

Both are proper scoring rules, so the only way to get the best reward is to report the true probabilities.

text:
This morning it finally came home to me. I will probably never write another program in C again.

Which is a big deal. I've been writing C since 1983. 43 years is a long time and a lot of skill investment. 

It's not like I didn't see this coming. I've been writing about the decline of C for years, predicting that it would be displaced by newer systems languages with better safety guarantees and more coherent designs.

It wasn't better language design alone that did it, though. It's how good LLMs now are at generating code from specs and prompts.

This means I can speak a program into existence in Rust or Go without any more effort than would be required to conjure it up in C. What makes this particularly dramatic is that I never learned to hand-code in Rust. And now - I don't need to.

What a long, strange trip it's been.

Crypto made 24/7 markets feel normal, but institutional collateral management still isn't.

That's a gap @Chainlink is currently closing as trillions of dollars of financial assets start to move onchain. Why?

> Exposures can change

Chainlink Fulcrum is designed to continuously monitor collateral and allow counterparties to respond according to their agreed terms.

24/7 assets require 24/7 financial infrastructure, and that's where Chainlink, and Fulcrum specifically, come in.
author: josefabregab
quoted_text:
Four days ago, @chainlink unveiled Fulcrum during Sibos.

Tier 1 financial institutions hold roughly $36.8B in excess or non-remunerated collateral. Think cash, Treasuries and other securities that have to be pre-positioned or left underutilized because collateral can't always move where it's needed, when it's needed.

Research from @Nasdaq and The ValueExchange (firm previously referenced in DTCC reports) estimates that tokenization could mobilize ~$4.8B of that collateral, generating ~$346M/year in additional interest income.

This makes the problem Chainlink Fulcrum is going after much easier to understand.

✖️ Collateral fragmented across custodians, venues and settlement windows.
✔️ Tokenized collateral movable across networks, available 24/7 and usable across financing venues.

The point isn't just putting collateral onchain, or tokenizing assets for the sake of tokenization. The goal is not leaving money on the table, and making balance sheets more versatile.

author: bubbleboi
quoted_text:
AI Drug Discovery Is Becoming a Bottleneck Trade

I get excited when an industry starts going through a real regime change. AI drug discovery (“AIDD”) increasingly looks like one of those moments.

Two things are happening:
1/ Upstream: the frontier AI labs are piling in.
2/ Downstream: The supply chain is clearly moving.

Supply-chain checks suggest the upstream picks-and-shovels of discovery and early preclinical R&D are starting to feel the increase in experimental volume.

DNA → protein → assays → sequencing → automation → preclinical testing

Names across that stack include $TWST , @GenScript , $ILMN , $TXG , lab-automation vendors and CROs.

$TWST expects triple-digit percentage growth in AI-enabled drug-discovery orders in FY26, and another year of triple-digit order growth in FY27.

@GenScript's AIDD business doubled YoY in 1H26. Its current platform advertises industrial-scale validation of 4,000+ designs/day, with integrated sequence-to-data workflows. Our channel checks suggest the ramp is moving even faster: roughly 8,000 designs/day currently, with a path toward ~16,000/day by YE26.

---
Why does AI drive more wet-lab demand?

1/ AI makes hypothesis generation almost free → way more shots on goal.
The bottleneck is moving from expert-driven design to biological validation.

2/ AI models need continuous experimental feedback — and both good and bad data are useful.
Traditionally, only the highest-conviction A+ candidates might get pushed into expensive validation. With AI, even the B/C candidates can be valuable because failed experiments generate training data.

@GenScript has said its sequence-to-binding workflow can return data in 4–7 days, and that faster cycle times matter because AI models depend on continuous experimental feedback.

@Anthropic is a clean example. @claudeai  designed 1,320 protein binders. @adaptyvbio  converted those digital sequences into DNA, expressed the proteins and tested binding. Only 354 actually bound. And the 966 failures are not wasted. They are useful negative labels: what does not express, what does not bind, what has poor affinity. Those results help train the next model iteration.

3/ Wet labs are no longer just making drugs. They are making training data.
$TWST  / @GenScript  increasingly look like biological data foundries.

$TWST explicitly talks about generating model-ready data from AI-designed sequences. In some workflows, the customer may care less about receiving the physical protein than about getting structured experimental results back into the model.

Traditional drug discovery asks: “Does candidate X work?”

AI drug discovery also asks: “What can this experiment teach the model?”

---
TAM of AIDD

If AI is simply a better R&D tool, the relevant spending pool is the $300–400B of annual global pharma R&D. If AI meaningfully increases the number of viable drug programs, the opportunity is larger because it expands downstream demand for DNA synthesis, protein production, assays, and preclinical work.

Near term, we can also size demand from AI-company spending. If Anthropic reaches $80B of ARR in 2026 and spends just 1% on AIDD, that alone would imply ~$800M of annual investment.

---
Trade setup

This is a trade that could have long legs. It’s hard to really stop working until PhaseI/II results (2028+)

It smells a lot like the bottleneck trade we just saw in semis: GPUs → HBM → networking → power/cooling. In biology, It basically follows the drug discovery process downstream: AI models → designs → DNA/protein → assays → preclinical capacity.

After the upstream picks-and-shovels, animal testing could become the next bottleneck. Monkey prices are already near prior highs and CRO capacity is tight. AIDD pushing more candidates into preclinical development would only add demand.

?? But clinical trials are still the bottleneck?
This is the biggest pushback I keep coming back to. No matter how fast discovery becomes, drugs still need to go through preclinical → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III → approval. You still need patients, time and capital.

But that doesn’t mean the bottleneck trade won’t work. More viable candidates — especially with higher success rates — still means more demand throughout the development process.

And who knows: clinical trials themselves may eventually be optimized by AI.

?? What breaks the trade?
Near term, the picks-and-shovels trade breaks if experimental budgets stop growing, AI-generated designs don’t translate into useful wet-lab hits, or capacity catches up too quickly.

Longer term, the thesis breaks if AI drugs look great in discovery / Phase I but fail at normal rates in Phase II/III. That is why Phase II matters so much.

?? Milestones
Late 2026–2027: first Isomorphic-designed drugs enter human trials; more AI-native programs move into IND-enabling work / tox.

2028–2030: clinical trial results start telling us whether AI-designed drugs actually perform better than conventional drugs.

Calling all the "bottleneck bros". :) @jukan05 @zephyr_z9 @aleabitoreddit @ParadisLabs

author: mcuban
quoted_text:
I'll even give you a preview @GovSherrillNJ 

My testimony today at the Texas State capital
I’m the co-founder of https://t.co/xY30tR9MWn.
We started Cost Plus Drugs because the prescription drug market is too complicated, too opaque and too expensive.
Our model is simple: we show what we pay for a drug, add a transparent markup and pharmacy fee, and show the customer the price.
No games. No hidden spread.
And a large percentage of our customers already have insurance.
They come to us because our cash price is often lower than what their insurance plan asks them to pay.
That tells you something is wrong.
Here are five things Texas can do about it.
1. Let patients shop for cheaper drugs
If someone's insurance says a prescription costs $500, but they can buy the exact same drug for $100 cash, let them buy it for $100.
Then credit that $100 toward their deductible and out-of-pocket maximum wherever Texas has authority to do so.
Patients should be rewarded for saving themselves and their health plan money.
They shouldn't be punished for it.
That's how you create something healthcare desperately needs:
Price competition.
2. Standardize PBM and TPA contracts
Texas should require the state, cities, counties and school districts to use standardized model contracts and mandatory terms for PBMs and TPAs.
I've reviewed these contracts.
They routinely run hundreds of pages.
I've seen contracting packages longer than a thousand pages.
There is no human being—or group of human beings—on this planet who can stay awake and understand every provision in contracts that complicated.
I don't care how much coffee they drink.
I call it contractual terrorism.
The vendor only has to sneak a couple of tricks through hundreds of pages.
The employer has to find every one.
It can't.
I've developed a model PBM contract designed to eliminate the major tricks and hidden economics we've identified.
Texas can have it for free.
Use mine. Improve it. Open source it.
I don't care.
Just stop making every government entity negotiate these contracts from scratch.
3. Make the economics public
If taxpayers are paying the bill, taxpayers should know the price.
Pricing. Fees. Rebates. Guarantees. Pharmacy reimbursement. Affiliate compensation. Audit rights.
Make them public.
I'm not talking about patient information or legitimate security information.
I'm talking about the money.
You cannot have an efficient market without price discovery.
Without price discovery, you get information asymmetry.
And when one side knows dramatically more than the other, guess who wins?
Not taxpayers.
Not employers.
Not patients.
Open the contracts up and let competitors see what they have to beat.
That giant sucking sound you hear will be money moving away from healthcare conglomerates that are too big to care and back toward taxpayers, employers and patients.
In the immortal words of Charles Barkley:
I guarantee it.
4. Kill the gag clauses
PBM contracts are like Fight Club.
The number one rule of Fight Club is that you can't talk about Fight Club.
The number one rule of many PBM contracts seems to be that you can't talk about your PBM contract.
That's insane.
Let employers compare pricing, rebates, fees, guarantees and reimbursement terms.
Markets work better when buyers know what other buyers are paying.
5. Make enforcement hurt
If a healthcare company commits a serious violation, give them one mulligan.
But after a second material federal or Texas enforcement action within a defined period, make them ineligible for new Texas government contracts for a period of time.
Two strikes.
You're out.
Today, some of these companies can make billions, get caught, pay a fine and write it off more easily than I wrote off an NBA fine.
That's not deterrence.
That's a cost of doing business.
And Texas should spend more on enforcement.
If Texas spends $10 million auditing contracts and analyzing claims and prevents $100 million in unnecessary spending, that's not overhead.

We’re already starting to see what kind of new jobs AI is creating. 

AI requires significant technical work and surrounding services to deploy into the economy. This means jobs for AI engineers that build applied AI products sold to (or within) enterprises, FDEs to deploy agents into companies, new services firms for deploying AI, and more. 

And even the published stats of new jobs undercount all the existing jobs that are transitioning to new areas of AI work in an enterprise. Many prior data, research, and software jobs large enterprises are also being repositioned for working with AI. 

Every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and even law firm is bringing on more technical talent -or repositioning existing roles- to help with agent deployment in their companies. It’s a lot easier to picture what AI can replace vs. what it creates until it starts happening. Now we’re seeing what this looks like.

The total true amount of Tasks done in outcome markets (like https://t.co/Hje8v8qD5b) is prob like 50k. This is a function of the immaturity of distributed swarms and agentic commerce technology . Swarm compute is a frontier design space that shifts with every model release. 

4. 
As models become more general, specialists of the past disappear. HOWEVER, specialists of the past that can understand how to imbue taste into their agents can now expose their skills to potential millions more clients. This is a key thesis of the Taskmarket design. And in a world of increasing slop - the benchmark of everything actually increases.

People don’t magically just get taste, it’s a skill that is refined over time, and why there is such a big opportunity for idea guys and tasteful designers that lean into outcome markets.

5.
Models are getting cheaper and faster at 100x per year approx, maybe even more so. But people will still demand quality and people will still pay for quality. And this quality will be surfaced on Taskmarkets - as it will be place where talent is discoverable via agent reputations. Every agent on the Taskmarket gets an identity that is 8004.

The faster, better and cheaper they get - the more markets are needed to surface talent. And there will be billions of agents on these markets and trillions of value eventually traded. 

6.
So as market penetration of agents across the economy happens at an accelerating rate, the amount of agents looking to complete work and post work increases. Numbers are about to get silly. Across every aspect of the agent stack, starting at hardware(already heavily constrained) then ending up in the agent economy. This is quite literally the global economy transitioning into an agent economy. 

7.
I came up with this conclusion about 12 months ago and we have been pushing in this vision. Building a protocol layer that enables these new markets to form, starting with the https://t.co/Hje8v8qD5b

I have longed every part of the stack, and my blood is in this protocol.

Every part of the stack has been designed to lean into this wild future that is coming. 

No constraints on the amount of participants to enter, BYO agent and soon to be released a way for anyone to launch their own swarm that can participate in this new economy with cloud agents that never sleep.

text:
刚看完  “PayPal 黑手党”核心人物，Palantir 联合创始人兼董事长、也是 Facebook 第一位外部投资人、《从 0 到 1》作者，彼得·蒂尔在 LBJ 总统图书馆讲台上的这段1分钟演讲，

作为一个在职场和大厂摸爬滚打了十几年的打工人，心里有种被当头棒喝的钝痛感，这种感觉好久都没退下去，

我们身边绝大多数受过良好教育的聪明人，从大学毕业那天起，几乎都在玩同一种看似极其合理的游戏：
 挑一份大厂或者咨询公司的光鲜工作，不是因为自己真的喜欢，而是因为写在简历上好看；
 去读个名校研究生，去考一堆行业证书，去拼命结交人脉，
 总觉得自己现在吃点苦、攒点背景没关系，只要手里的筹码足够多，以后就会有更好的选项。

但彼得·蒂尔在视频里极其冷峻地撕开了这个困住无数精英的温水陷阱：
 如果你把未来看成是不确定的，你就会把整个人生规划成一棵不断分叉的树， 你用一辈子的时间去攒简历、去争取做某件事的资格，却可能到死都没有真正开工去过那种你真正想要的生活。

他把我们衡量一份工作或一条路的视角，极其锋利地切成了三个时间尺度：
第一个是极短期，你现在每天到底开不开心？手头做的事能不能让你高速学到硬核东西？
 第二个是中期，这东西写在简历上好不好看？能不能变成跳槽去下一家公司的体面门票？
 第三个是极长期，你现在做的事，放在未来十年二十年的尺度上，到底是不是一件真正重要、有价值的事？

蒂尔点出了这个世界最畸形的一个真相： 今天的社会评价体系，严重过度奖励了中期， 大家把 80% 的精力都耗费在刷简历、攒背书、做精致的利己主义者上； 而恰恰低估了极短期和极长期的组合。

中期所谓的保持选项开放，在很多时候只是一种高智商的懦弱与逃避。 你用以后再说这句看似成熟的借口，廉价地出卖了当下的热情，也彻底放弃了在极长期的重要方向上死磕的勇气。

蒂尔给出的校准建议极度干脆： 彻底把中期忘掉，把你的全部精力重新分配给极短期和极长期。
 要么去干一件能让你每天醒来都极度兴奋、能疯狂学到东西的酷事； 要么选定一个哪怕再难、但未来十年一定极其重要的确定方向，然后从今天第一秒就全仓押上动手去干。
人生最昂贵的成本，从来不是走错路的学费，
 而是你在漫长的资格准备中，把最宝贵的黄金岁月全部耗在了为下一轮表演攒门票上。

视频下一条高赞评论说得极其扎心： 我们花了一辈子的时间去证明自己有资格做某件事，却始终没有真正开始过那种生活。

换作是你，如果把写在简历上好不好看这层顾虑彻底撕掉，你今天最想立刻动手开工干的第一件事是什么？

其实早年我花了五年在大厂攒资历，后来发现那些看似光鲜的职级标签，加起来还不如自己当年熬夜写出来的一个独立开源小工具让我感到真实和踏实。 https://t.co/hER2jJg9uF

> under 1.8% regressions on correct branches

Astra explores the maze. Opus repairs the logic

text:
低成本做AI应用，用Cloudflare这一套就够了🔥

很多人以为做AI 工具要花钱，其实 Cloudflare 已经把大部分基础设施配好了

1、Workers

负责 API、业务逻辑和 Agent 调度，可以直接当 AI 应用的后端。

2、Workers AI

直接跑 Llama、Qwen、Gemma 等模型，自带免费额度，做 Demo 和小工具很方便。

3、AI Gateway

把 OpenAI、Claude、Gemini 等模型接口统一接进来，日志、缓存、限流、调用统计一起解决。

4、Vectorize

Cloudflare 自己的向量数据库，知识库、RAG、语义搜索都能直接用。

5、D1 + KV

D1 存用户、任务和结构化数据，KV 放配置、缓存和一些高频状态。

6、R2 + Queues

R2 存图片、文档和模型素材，Queues 负责异步任务，避免耗时操作一直卡着请求。

这样下来：

模型 → API → RAG → 数据库 → 文件 → 异步任务

一套 AI 应用需要的大部分东西，基本都能放在 Cloudflare。

而且很多服务都有免费额度，前期做 Demo、个人项目、小型 SaaS 都够用，真正有用户以后再按需升级就行
author: xiaomovps
quoted_text:
低成本建站，用Cloudflare 这一套就够了🔥

很多人都是在考虑建站，但是很多时候都在考虑成本，其实 Cloudflare 已经给你提供了所有免费的资源

我帮你总结好了：

1、DNS + CDN + SSL

域名接进 Cloudflare，解析、CDN、HTTPS 一次解决，基本是所有网站的第一步

2、Pages / Workers

纯前端、博客、文档站直接 Pages；需要 API、后端逻辑，就上 Workers。

3、D1 数据库

用户、文章、配置这些结构化数据直接放 D1，小项目完全够用

4、R2 存图片和文件

图片、附件、视频、备份都丢 R2，最舒服的是出站流量基本不收费。

5、Turnstile 防机器人

注册、登录、评论、表单直接加 Turnstile，不用自己折腾验证码。

6、Email Routing 收邮件

hello@你的域名 直接转发到 Gmail / Outlook，做联系邮箱足够了。

邮件也可以直接在 Cloudflare 上买好，这样下来 建站的 CDN、SSL、域名邮箱、数据库、图床，基本上你能想到的他都有

而且免费额度给得很足，如果实在用的不够的话 可以根据对应的服务去升级，不管是小白练手，还是项目初期阶段都是非常好的

1. 临时的新加坡本地网络和电话有两种，一种是只有流量的，基本都是 esim 这种不需要 KYC ，但也不能打电话和收短信，只能提供流量，总的来说就是没有 +65 的功能。

另一种就是游客卡，主要就是短期的，需要 KYC ，可以在 7-11 等买，或者直接在机场买也可以，可以获得 +65 的功能。

对于部分小伙伴来说，买一个然后注册一些网站是可以的，这种卡一般最多用30天。

推荐用 Singtel 的游客卡，大概 10新币（53人民币不到）、7天有效期、500GB 新加坡/马来西亚/印尼/泰国/香港流量，5G，并包含本地无限通话和短信。实体 SIM 和 eSIM 都有。

非常适合在新加坡以后想要去马来西亚的小伙伴，可以不用换卡了，直接就能在马来西亚用。

2. 入境卡一定要填写，非常快，很好写，基本上填好后 30 分钟内就能收到邮件，收到邮件就可以过关了，新加坡过关效率很高，不用担心。

新加坡过海关不需要小费，没有任何的人工检索通道（小黑屋除外），都是自动机器，非常快。

3. 新加坡入境不能带电子烟，千万别带，电子烟在新加坡是违法的，最好也不要带烟，新加坡烟草管制非常严格，从来不存在一个人可以带 X 支烟这样的说法，哪怕带一根都需要申报。

我知道会有小伙伴会说自己每次都偷偷带，对，不被发现是没事，但如果被发现就会比较麻烦，尤其是带多了点就会当走私处理了。

另外进入新加坡可以带酒，一般来说 500ML 的白酒可以带两瓶，威士忌可以带 1L ，喜欢喝酒的小伙伴出来海关酒可以看到卖酒的，价格还算可以，如果有打折的话当年茅台大概是 230 多新币，没打折的话大概小 300 新币吧。

新加坡买烟在超市也可以买，但烟不会摆在外边，需要自己和售货员说，然后才能买，我不抽烟，所以也不知道都有什么品牌，听说基本都是万宝路。

4. 新加坡换钱挺容易的，汇率也还算过的去，在牛车水（中国街）有很多换汇公司，甚至可以从微信换成新币，也可以把人民币寄回中国，但听说偶尔会出现冻卡。

我个人建议来新加坡还是要带一些现金的，因为并不是所有地方都可以刷信用卡，尤其是小贩中心或者食阁，如果没有新加坡本地的支付方式，现金是最好的。

汇率大概是不到 5.3 元人民币换 1 新币，一般来说小贩中心或者亚坤这类的吃吃一个人大概要 15 新币左右，如果是食阁的话，一碗面大概是 6 新币，一份蛋炒饭大概是 5.5 新币，一份海南鸡大概是 8 新币。

另外新加坡的地铁可以直接用 VISA 和 Mastercard卡，刷了就可以走，应该是按距离收费的，起手点应该是 1 新币左右，我基本做一站都是 1.0X 新币左右。

5. 很多短视频都有介绍新加坡的规矩特别多，动不动就罚款，也对，也不对，确实规矩很多，但也不是非常容易被罚款，一般来说第一次发现都是会警告一下，比如室外没有在规定的地方抽烟。

对，新加坡地铁，公交和出租车上都不能吃东西和喝水，有时候出租车还好，但公众交通如果被发现，对方还是较真的人，确实是挺麻烦的。

总的来说自己都认为不是好事的，就别做，那就肯定没错了。

6. 新加坡的打车其实非常容易，但刚刚来新加坡可能会觉得不方便，首先是打车不能扬招，其次打车都需要去打车点（pickup point），没有在的话，就要自己找，另外新加坡打车基本上有 3 分钟的等待时间，超过时间就要扣超时费。

新加坡最好用的还是 Grab ，尤其是从机场出来的时候，Grab 的性价比要高于出租车，Grab 可以绑定信用卡，而且在新加坡还可以用 USDT 充值（我不记得游客是否可以了），总之 Grab 是挺好用的。

如果看到司机是华人面孔可以尝试说中文，大多数都会讲中文，如果是看到印度裔等那就只能说英文了。

7. 在新加坡大多数的路边店是没有什么“服务”概念的， 尤其是吃饭的时候别指望能有多周到的服务，但相比香港还是强多了，当然也会有部分服务员素质不高的情况，能不吵架尽量就别吵架。

一般的饭店都有 10% 的服务费 和 9% 的税，都含在账单里的，所以不用给小费。新加坡几乎没有小费文化。

8. 如果在新加坡有什么问题，而且恰好你又有我的联系方式，可以联系我，力所能及的帮忙还是没问题的。

还有什么是我遗漏的？

一个 @Gate ，交易更多市场

text:
最近准备切换到 Building 模式，所以接下来看项目可能不会像之前那么深入。

不过最近新项目还是不少的。把近期扫到、觉得可以再看看的几个分享出来：有实名或半实名 dev，也有身份还没确认、但或许值得研究的匿名项目。

只是初筛线索，不是完整尽调，也不是投资推荐。具体细节请自行研究。

1.xCoin官网：https://t.co/UIrxvQP90p：David Otero／SystemThreat。其公开介绍列为 DLT 创始人，涉及链、矿工、钱包和基础设施开发；履历主要来自本人自述。

2.TalCash官网：https://t.co/G2TnnZo25C：Tal Ben Arie／talbenarie。个人简介自述是 TechnoTal 创始人，做游戏及客户端／服务端软件开发，项目经历包括 Shinobi Warfare。

3.CommonFoundry官网：https://t.co/Tg1bqp7VeH目前追到的维护账号是 JustAResearcher，实名和职业履历尚未确认。项目探索矩阵运算 PoW 与 AI 推理方向，技术主张仍需进一步验证。

4.Hegemon官网：https://t.co/iIGOC6sWfF背后是 Pauli Group。其创始人 Pierre-Luc Dallaire-Demers 的机构简介列有理论物理博士、Harvard 博后，以及 Xanadu、Zapata 的量子算法研究经历，背景与后量子方向比较相关。

5.Proxima官方文档网站：https://t.co/zko61bTpul
GitHub：https://t.co/4fyRtJoyOk：Evaldas Drąsutis／lunfardo314。IOTA 历史官方记录明确列其为智能合约协议 ISCP 负责人，有可追溯的分布式账本研发经历。

6. Trust Stack Network官网：https://t.co/seYd53wTHT官网明确采用化名团队，列有 Vince.K、Kai.V 等角色。真实身份和既往职业履历尚未确认，不能把官网列出的头衔当成已经核实的背景。

7.QuDAG GitHub：https://t.co/yVRUyyStEu
开发者网站：https://t.co/ai7214axsY（未确认独立项目官网）主要公开人物是 Reuven Cohen，即 rUv／ruvnet。公开履历包括创办 Enomaly、联合创办 CloudCamp，属于云计算创业和 AI 工程背景，不直接等同于密码学研究资历。

8.SHEAR官网：https://t.co/PRUJmqT4U3：Russell G Sneddon／Raskul。有 隐私币 Beam 生态经历，Beam 历史官方报道记录了他的开源矿池贡献。准确说是有矿工社区与矿池建设经历，不直接称“前 Beam 核心协议开发者”。

9.Primechain 仓库  https://t.co/KbB5nsSy7D
Dev：Ovanes Oganisian，MidLincoln Research 公开资料列其为创始人，背景主要是投资策略与量化研究，也是项目白皮书联合作者。

单看公开人物和技术履历，我个人觉得 Proxima 和 Hegemon 的开发者背景相对不错，更值得继续花时间跟踪。当然，履历不错不代表项目一定能成，代码、安全、经济模型和实际网络情况还是要单独研究。

最后纯信息免费共享，社区送温暖。如果你从这些线索里发现机会、还有幸赚到了钱，记得回来给我打赏一下 😄

另外如果你也发现了好项目、好机会，记得私信发过来提醒我，大家互通有无，谢谢老师们。

MAYBE capital is scarce (expensive) this time because the opportunity set got dramatically better? If AI creates a huge number of high-return places to deploy capital (compute, power, datacenters, robotics, new companies), everyone wants capital to build them.

text:
AI Drug Discovery Is Becoming a Bottleneck Trade

I get excited when an industry starts going through a real regime change. AI drug discovery (“AIDD”) increasingly looks like one of those moments.

Two things are happening:
1/ Upstream: the frontier AI labs are piling in.
2/ Downstream: The supply chain is clearly moving.

Supply-chain checks suggest the upstream picks-and-shovels of discovery and early preclinical R&D are starting to feel the increase in experimental volume.

DNA → protein → assays → sequencing → automation → preclinical testing

Names across that stack include $TWST , @GenScript , $ILMN , $TXG , lab-automation vendors and CROs.

$TWST expects triple-digit percentage growth in AI-enabled drug-discovery orders in FY26, and another year of triple-digit order growth in FY27.

@GenScript's AIDD business doubled YoY in 1H26. Its current platform advertises industrial-scale validation of 4,000+ designs/day, with integrated sequence-to-data workflows. Our channel checks suggest the ramp is moving even faster: roughly 8,000 designs/day currently, with a path toward ~16,000/day by YE26.

---
Why does AI drive more wet-lab demand?

1/ AI makes hypothesis generation almost free → way more shots on goal.
The bottleneck is moving from expert-driven design to biological validation.

2/ AI models need continuous experimental feedback — and both good and bad data are useful.
Traditionally, only the highest-conviction A+ candidates might get pushed into expensive validation. With AI, even the B/C candidates can be valuable because failed experiments generate training data.

@GenScript has said its sequence-to-binding workflow can return data in 4–7 days, and that faster cycle times matter because AI models depend on continuous experimental feedback.

@Anthropic is a clean example. @claudeai  designed 1,320 protein binders. @adaptyvbio  converted those digital sequences into DNA, expressed the proteins and tested binding. Only 354 actually bound. And the 966 failures are not wasted. They are useful negative labels: what does not express, what does not bind, what has poor affinity. Those results help train the next model iteration.

3/ Wet labs are no longer just making drugs. They are making training data.
$TWST  / @GenScript  increasingly look like biological data foundries.

$TWST explicitly talks about generating model-ready data from AI-designed sequences. In some workflows, the customer may care less about receiving the physical protein than about getting structured experimental results back into the model.

Traditional drug discovery asks: “Does candidate X work?”

AI drug discovery also asks: “What can this experiment teach the model?”

---
TAM of AIDD

If AI is simply a better R&D tool, the relevant spending pool is the $300–400B of annual global pharma R&D. If AI meaningfully increases the number of viable drug programs, the opportunity is larger because it expands downstream demand for DNA synthesis, protein production, assays, and preclinical work.

Near term, we can also size demand from AI-company spending. If Anthropic reaches $80B of ARR in 2026 and spends just 1% on AIDD, that alone would imply ~$800M of annual investment.

---
Trade setup

This is a trade that could have long legs. It’s hard to really stop working until PhaseI/II results (2028+)

It smells a lot like the bottleneck trade we just saw in semis: GPUs → HBM → networking → power/cooling. In biology, It basically follows the drug discovery process downstream: AI models → designs → DNA/protein → assays → preclinical capacity.

After the upstream picks-and-shovels, animal testing could become the next bottleneck. Monkey prices are already near prior highs and CRO capacity is tight. AIDD pushing more candidates into preclinical development would only add demand.

?? But clinical trials are still the bottleneck?
This is the biggest pushback I keep coming back to. No matter how fast discovery becomes, drugs still need to go through preclinical → Phase I → Phase II → Phase III → approval. You still need patients, time and capital.

But that doesn’t mean the bottleneck trade won’t work. More viable candidates — especially with higher success rates — still means more demand throughout the development process.

And who knows: clinical trials themselves may eventually be optimized by AI.

?? What breaks the trade?
Near term, the picks-and-shovels trade breaks if experimental budgets stop growing, AI-generated designs don’t translate into useful wet-lab hits, or capacity catches up too quickly.

Longer term, the thesis breaks if AI drugs look great in discovery / Phase I but fail at normal rates in Phase II/III. That is why Phase II matters so much.

?? Milestones
Late 2026–2027: first Isomorphic-designed drugs enter human trials; more AI-native programs move into IND-enabling work / tox.

2028–2030: clinical trial results start telling us whether AI-designed drugs actually perform better than conventional drugs.

Calling all the "bottleneck bros". :) @jukan05 @zephyr_z9 @aleabitoreddit @ParadisLabs 

+++
More comprehensive analysis: https://t.co/vaTuiyyYB6

卧槽，美联储降息预期砸到了12%，本月比特币冲刺 $90,000+ ？

这周宏观最大的变化，是市场对美联储 10 月继续加息的预期被连续打下来了。

周初公布的职位空缺降到 707.9 万，低于预期。

今晚非农更狠，9 月只新增 2.9 万人，市场预期 9 万，失业率反而从 4.1% 升到 4.2%。

工资环比也只有 +0.1%，同比 +3.0%，劳动力市场正在明显降温。

本周初市场一度给到约 70% 的 10 月加息概率，今晚非农出来后，一度被砸到 12%，随后回到约 19%。

10 年美债收益率也从本周最高 5.34% 附近快速回落到 5.16% 左右。

然后油价又来了一波助攻。

欧洲正在讨论释放 5000 万桶柴油储备，同时推动 IEA 成员释放约 5000 万桶原油，Brent 已经重新跌破 $100，WTI 跌到 $90 下方。

油价往下走，能源通胀压力就往下走，美联储 10 月继续加息的理由又少了一块。

author: zephyr_z9
quoted_text:
Deep| $Ibiden: The Substrate Seller’s Market Has Only Just Begun
High-end ABF capacity still failing to keep pace with the area and layer count of AI silicon

Ibiden’s (4062 JP) core driver remains qualified high-end ABF capacity failing to keep pace with the area and layer count of AI silicon. Intel/AMD server CPU shipments grow +36%/+62% in 2027 on new platforms 56–63% larger in substrate area, widening the CPU gap further. GPUs and EMIB-T consume the highest-end capacity: Rubin yields only 12 units per panel, TPU V9 / Trainium 4 only 4. The next pricing step falls on 27Q1 contract renewals, where new products can price above legacy agreements. We forecast FY3/27 / FY3/28 revenue growth of 35% / 30% and EPS of JPY173 / JPY267; at ~45x FY3/28E PE the shares still have rerating room, with the FY27Q2 results call the near-term catalyst.

-CPU demand is back and widens the supply gap. Resident agents such as Muse push workloads back onto CPUs via headless browsers and high-frequency API calls, and Intel can currently fill only ~50% of orders; shipments have upside if capacity allows. FUNDA models Intel server CPU shipments of 26.5mn units in 2027E (+36%) and AMD 20.4mn (+62%); multiplied by substrate area 63% larger for Diamond Rapids vs. Granite Rapids and 56% larger for Venice vs. Turin, substrate-area demand grows far faster than unit count. Supply is not only limited but already allocated: tier-1 and tier-2 makers are all full as of 26Q4, lead times are 48–52 weeks, total 2027 capacity grows only ~10–15%, and a visible shortfall opens from 27Q1. Customers that did not co-fund capacity sit lower in the allocation queue. This is already visible at Ibiden: AMD substrate revenue declines sequentially through 2H FY3/27 as capacity temporarily allocated to AMD returns to Intel; this does not reflect weaker AMD demand.

-GPUs and EMIB-T consume the highest-end slice of capacity. Blackwell is 73×81mm at 14 layers; Rubin 83×97mm at 18 layers, an estimated 1.8x the area; Rubin Ultra more than 2x Blackwell’s area at ~3x the price. EMIB-T is more extreme: Google TPU V9 at ~120×120mm, 24 layers with a multi-layer core, and Amazon Trainium 4 at ~120×120mm, 24 layers with a multi-layer core, each yielding only 4 substrates per panel. Even if ASIC unit growth looks modest, what truly consumes capacity is area, layer count and yield (core-stage yield on a multi-layer core drops from 99.9% to 97–98%, and a core defect can render all subsequent build-up layers worthless).

-Substrate price increases continue, supporting Ibiden’s new-product pricing. This year’s increases came mainly from Taiwanese makers; Ibiden only removed its quarterly price-decline assumption and normalized Intel pricing to a fair level. Next year, with the industry shortfall in place and lead times at 48–52 weeks, the next customer contract renewals fall in 27Q1 and new products can secure better quotes; new T-glass suppliers are also expected to qualify in 27Q1, and with Chinese and Taiwanese suppliers raising prices Ibiden also has room to pass through costs, while substrates remain under 10% of chip cost so we expect customers to accept the increase. We have not yet seen specific quotes, but we think a price increase is likely.

text:
I spent the last week in Toronto at OMERS AI Assembly, hosted by @HenryGladwyn, with some of the largest allocators in the world and the people building and funding the AI buildout.

I had the privilege of moderating a conversation with my buddy @PhilipJohnston, cofounder and CEO of @Starcloud_, on next-generation power and data centers in space. The agenda was a stacked lineup of some of the most influential investors in the business, including @GavinSBaker, @AltCap, @htaneja, Ben Horowitz, @vkhosla, Neil Shah, Jared Middleman, Nabil Mallick, and others.

Tons of food for thought, but worth sharing a few takeaways:

• The AI buildout is a physics problem. Power, heat, copper and chip supply came up far more than models did. The founders solving atoms will set the pace for everyone else.

• Every software company eventually goes physical. Hearing a search company talk about investing in journalists to verify information was one of the more surprising moments of the summit.

• Venture firms are being rebuilt too. Agents running first-pass diligence, a "shadow brain" for every person on the team. The work that stays human is judgment and relationships, which is exactly where I want to spend my time. (Cerebro at 776 was ahead of its time, but I was glad to hear we're still leading the pack!)

Thank you to Henry and the OMERS Ventures team, @OTPPinfo, and @chao_helena for bringing this room together. Grateful to be part of it.

text:
I built an AI slop machine over the weekend. I will never launch it, after seeing what I created.

You put in a story prompt, and it generates a more structured story with stakes, cliffhangers, a beginning, middle, end. Splits it into episodes. Storyboards the whole thing, makes a cast, music, poster, voiceovers. Then generates the visuals (different styles available from anime to cinematic) and you can play the episode as a slideshow, or render it as a video. Uses all the latest models that you would expect.

A few observations from this exercise:

1) it was trivial to build

There's no moat here. This is just "AI glue", building an app that wraps several AI models. The moat is the GTM strategy, which leads me to...

2) this space is insanely competitive

there's tons of AI movie makers all using the same models with some thin layer of prompt direction or UX as the differentiation. totally saturated.

3) AI video courses

I noticed that some of the biggest advertisers in this space are people selling "how to create your own AI movie" courses. There's something off about this, almost dropshippy. It suggests that there's more value in hyping the thing and selling courses about the thing, than there is in the thing.

4) this shit is really expensive

All of those cool AI videos that you see using the latest video models, are expensive to make. A 60 second "mini episode" of a story built using my platform would cost $5 in raw inference. There's no business here, whatever margin you put on top of that can just get eaten by a competitor. And imagine if a user buys $100 of credits (of which $90 is passed through to your AI provider) then decides they hate the movie that was created, and asks for a refund or charges back. Enough of those in a month will bankrupt you.

5) just didn't feel right

It's a fun little demo that got some laughs from my friends but ultimately it's contributing to the never ending pile of AI slop. Is that something I want to be part of? Not really.

text:
“评论云、存储、芯片、光模块等上面的标的，哪些是攻守兼备的好标的？哪些的弹性最大适合做波段？”

看了AI给的分析， 我觉大部分建议挺合理的

结论： “底仓仍放台积电和博通，英伟达可以加重。谷歌是云里的压舱。波段仓给存储三只，SK海力士赔率最清楚，闪迪弹性最大。光模块里只留Coherent做波段，Lumentum等回落到均值下方再看。AMD、英特尔、Nebius只做事件。” 

云
谷歌还是云里唯一接近攻守兼备的。343.50美元，滚动17.7倍 ，是巨型股里最便宜的，目标均值431美元，大约还有两成半空间。2027年市盈率23.4倍，说明近端盈利没有加速，进攻性一般，适合压舱。

微软517.53美元，2027年22.3倍，目标约566美元，上行不到一成。守得住，不适合做波段。

亚马逊251.52美元、2027年23.9倍，弹性在AWS资本开支。Meta 728.08美元、2027年21.5倍，弹性在广告周期和开支指引。两只都是中性，不是底仓首选，也不是高弹性。（我个人倒认为Meta 属于高弹性和AI的分析有分歧）

甲骨文142.30美元、2027年12.9倍、2028年约9.6倍，目标均值238美元，纸面空间最大。自由现金流和云执行仍是缺口，更像“事件股”，不是攻守兼备。

Nebius 242.81美元，目标84–415美元，没有盈利锚，纯情绪。SpaceX 158.96美元、约108倍远期，星链是故事，不是现在的利润。（我个人认为SpaceX倒是弹性不小的成长股，市场情绪影响很大）

存储
三只仍不是底仓。便宜是周期顶定价，不是安全边际 （这个我个人也不认同，因为“这一次不一样”）。美光1,074.89美元，2027年6.7倍、2028年约6.3倍，目标361–2,200美元，卖方自己没有共识。

闪迪1,719.99美元，是这组里少数回落的，2027年6.6–8.0倍，目标1,000–3,600美元。

SK海力士ADR 195.13美元，2027年4.3倍、2028年约4.0倍，目标163–562美元、均值333美元，上行约七成，是三只里赔率最清楚的。

弹性排序不变：闪迪大于美光大于SKHY。
闪迪市值较小、业绩从深亏拉出来，单季指引就能甩开。
美光是数据和报价驱动的标准波段。
SKHY有HBM份额，ADR比韩股好交易，但波动仍由合约价决定。价格能守住，只有HBM和NAND不塌。

芯片
台积电仍是整张表里最好的攻守。472.78美元，2027年21.6倍、2028年约16.5倍，目标均值541美元，还有大约14%空间。先进制程不可替代，弹性中等，不适合当主波段。

博通是芯片里的攻守。355.14美元，2027年18.6倍、2028年约11.2倍，目标均值517美元，上行约46%。定制ASIC加软件现金流，比英伟达更守，比云厂商更有订单弹性。光模块这两天大涨之后，博通的相对赔率更好。

英伟达233.95美元，2027年15.0倍、2028年约8.8倍，目标275–515美元、均值343美元，上行约47%。大型算力股里远期仍最便宜。可以当核心，也可以围绕财报做波段。

AMD 633.91美元，2027年40.2倍，目标均值581美元，低于现价。弹性高，趋势赔率差，只做相对强弱，不做底仓。

英特尔119.33美元，2027年56.3倍，平均目标110美元仍低于现价。事件波段，不是基本面趋势。

光模块
Lumentum两天从约971美元涨到1,085.42美元，2027年约48倍，2028年约27–30倍。卖方均值1,073美元，已经低于现价，区间240–1,400美元说明离散极大。
弹性还是最大，但已经从“有估值支撑的波段”变成“动量过冲”。再做只能博订单和指引继续上修，不能按目标价当安全垫。

Coherent从约288美元涨到337.04美元，2027年从20.5倍抬到24.0倍，2028年约16倍。均值395美元、高点500美元，还有大约17%到均值。弹性仍大，赔率比Lumentum好，但入场比两天前差一截。

迈威尔272.29美元，2027年40.5倍、2028年约24.7倍，目标均值291美元，上行只剩约7%。弹性还在，安全边际没了，不适合重仓波段。

用法
底仓仍放台积电和博通，英伟达可以加重。谷歌是云里的压舱。波段仓给存储三只，SKHY赔率最清楚，闪迪弹性最大。光模块里只留Coherent做波段，Lumentum等回落到均值下方再看。AMD、英特尔、Nebius只做事件。

苹果333.69美元、2027年34.7倍，目标均值338美元，这张表里既不攻也不适合波段。定价，攻守兼备和波段弹性是两类完全不同的东西。便宜不等于能守，贵也不等于弹性大。 $TSM  $AVGO  $NVDA

text:
OpenAI 刚出了一份 GPT-6 家族实用指南，我觉得对经常用 Codex 的人非常有用。

它把三个模型的分工讲得很清楚。

Astra 留给最难的推理、Coding 和复杂专业任务；GPT-6.1 Sol 负责大部分需要质量又要考虑成本的复杂工作；Luna 更适合高频、明确、重复性的任务。

推理档位也一样。

提取、分类、简单修改可以从 low 开始；Debug、规划、代码推理再上 medium / high；xhigh 和 max 最好等 Eval 证明真的值得再开。OpenAI 甚至明确提醒，推理档位更高并不保证结果一定更好。

我以前用 Codex 也很容易犯这个毛病，一上来就把最强模型和最高推理档位拉满。

但很多任务其实根本吃不完这些算力，只会多花时间和额度。

以后用 Coding Agent，模型和 reasoning effort 也应该像算力调度一样按任务分配。

text:
很多人还没意识到，MCP Events 可能是近期 AI Agent 领域最被低估的核心更新。

目前绝大多数人的 Agent 本质上仍然是“被动型”的： 要么是你主动去聊天框敲一句 Prompt 把它们叫醒； 要么是通过死板的定时任务（Cron Job）不停轮询。
但事件驱动（Event-Driven）的标准化，正在彻底重塑 Agent 的唤醒逻辑——从“人去找 AI”转向“环境状态主动触发 AI”。
有人可能会问：“这不就是存在了多年的 Webhook 吗？” 原理上类似，但关键在于协议与大模型上下文的标准化打通。过去你很难让外部业务事件直接、原生且低门槛地唤醒 ChatGPT 或 Claude。一旦事件总线与协议铺平，几个场景将迎来质变：

工作流中的原生协作者：在 Notion、Google Docs、Figma 或 Linear 中直接 @Agent，它不再只是个死板的机器人脚本，而是能立刻捕捉上下文并直接执行复杂编辑与任务。

智能分流与前置执行：监听 Slack 消息、紧急邮件或 GitHub PR。Agent 不仅做通知，还能在打扰你之前，就完成优先级研判、草拟回复或前置跑完初步检查。
“子代理即服务”（Subagent-as-a-Service）生态：主 Agent 充当统筹中枢，垂直领域的专业 Agent（如法律合规、特定领域数据校验）作为事件驱动的专属模块按需介入，形成真正的多智能体异步协作。

从“问答式工具”跨越到“自主数字员工”，真正的分水岭不仅在于底层模型有多聪明，更在于它究竟是永远在等人类下令，还是具备了对环境变化做出响应的神经反射弧。

text:
Jay Clayton was just named Trump’s AI czar and will lead the new “Super Intelligence Force”… which is interesting to say the least.

I interviewed Clayton in 2022, shortly after he left the SEC and the agency sued Ripple over XRP, and then heard him speak in 2023 at a conference.

Looking back at those conversations now, it’s interesting how much has changed and what the throughline here could be.

In 2022, Clayton told me, “I see digital assets, whether [they are] in the form of a tokenized traditional security, a stablecoin or a new type of asset, being part of our global infrastructure.” He was right about that.

He also said that the combination of tokenization and smart contracts could bring efficiency to existing financial infrastructure and create access to additional markets. Again, he was right about that.

Then in 2023, while arguing that many tokens would fall under the definition of securities, he said, “The regulatory sector needs to come to grips with the fact that we are going to have interoperability. We are going to have programmable assets operate much more efficiently. That’s going to happen.”

He was right about the direction of the technology. But the regulatory classification around a lot of the assets themselves has changed substantially since then, with the SEC and CFTC now classifying a number of major crypto assets as digital commodities rather than securities. 

While those conversations were about crypto and securities regulation, now the technology in question is AI and Clayton will be responsible for assessing both its risks and opportunities over the next 120 days. 

Interestingly, during his confirmation hearing for DNI, Clayton described AI as “not only an opportunity but a threat.”

He added, when “something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it.”

Obviously, crypto and AI are very different technologies. But having reported on Clayton during one of crypto’s biggest regulatory hurdles, I’ll be interested to see how that same focus on technology, infra, regulation and risk carries into his approach to AI.

I spent the last week in Toronto at OMERS AI Assembly, hosted by @HenryGladwyn, with some of the largest allocators in the world and the people building and funding the AI buildout.

I had the privilege of moderating a conversation with my buddy @PhilipJohnston, cofounder and CEO of @Starcloud_, on next-generation power and data centers in space. The agenda was a stacked lineup of some of the most influential investors in the business, including @GavinSBaker, @AltCap, @htaneja, Ben Horowitz, @vkhosla, Neil Shah, Jared Middleman, Nabil Mallick, and others.

Tons of food for thought, but worth sharing a few takeaways:

• The AI buildout is a physics problem. Power, heat, copper and chip supply came up far more than models did. The founders solving atoms will set the pace for everyone else.

• Every software company eventually goes physical. Hearing a search company talk about investing in journalists to verify information was one of the more surprising moments of the summit.

• Venture firms are being rebuilt too. Agents running first-pass diligence, a "shadow brain" for every person on the team. The work that stays human is judgment and relationships, which is exactly where I want to spend my time. (Cerebro at 776 was ahead of its time, but I was glad to hear we're still leading the pack!)

Thank you to Henry and the OMERS Ventures team, @OTPPinfo, and @chao_helena for bringing this room together. Grateful to be part of it.

text:
最近 Vitalik 推荐了下 zkAPI，简单看了下 Open Anonymity Project 的 zkAPI，简单理解就是：把“谁付的钱”和“谁在调用 API”拆开。

为什么要拆？

现在使用 AI 服务，账号、付款和提问通常连在一起：

你的付款身份
    ↓
你的账号 / API Key
    ↓
一次次模型请求
    ↓
可以持续积累的个人画像

尤其是 Personal Agent，知道你的工作、财务、关系和生活习惯。单次提问可能没什么，但长期拼起来就可能还原你的画像。

zkAPI 解决的是：服务商需要确认你付得起钱，但不一定需要知道你是谁、对应哪笔充值。

以 OA 的 AI 使用场景为例，简化流程是：

【付款与授权】

钱包存入 ETH
    ↓
浏览器生成零知识证明
“我有足够余额支付”
但不直接透露对应哪笔存款
    ↓
授权服务验证证明
    ↓
获得短期使用凭证

【模型请求】

问题 + 短期凭证
    ↓
OpenRouter
    ↓
模型提供商
    ↓
返回回答，按用量计费（应该是服务商代付）

这里零知识证明的作用，让你能证明“我有资格使用”，不是加密你的 Prompt。也就是说，模型仍然看得到你问了什么，但这次请求不用通过一个长期绑定付款身份的账号来授权。

我觉得这个方向有意思的地方在于，它试图把付费 API 里习以为常的“付款、身份、使用记录绑定”，拆成更少暴露信息的流程。不只是 AI，类似思路也可以用于 RPC、数据接口等服务。所以它叫 zkAPI。

不过，拆链路是手段，不等于自动实现匿名。如果你在提示词里写了姓名、公司和邮箱，内容本身就可能暴露身份；IP、请求时间等元数据也不会因为用了 ZK 就自动消失。存取款的链上记录同样公开可见。所以 Vitalik 这里用本地模型构造请求，用 Tor 减少网络层追踪。

这其实也从第一性原理提供了解决隐私问题的方案，其实有点混币器的思路，不一定只能对内容加密，对整个流程拆分、混淆也是可以的，增加匹配难度。
author: brucexu_eth
quoted_text:
Doing a bit of a self-experiment.

Goal: use my personal health and travel data to provide personalized diet and exercise recommendations for me, using frontier models but in a way that avoids leaking to them any private information.

Strategy: use a local model (Qwen 3.8 Flash Next) to orchestrate, and use powerful remote models as a tool call to benefit from higher-level thinking and knowledge that the local model does not have.

Three-layer approach to privacy:

Avoid leaking personally identifiable information, or leaking my identity through writing style -> local model writes the queries to the frontier model, not me
Avoid leaking who I am through the payment channel -> zkAPI
Avoid leaking who I am through networking / IP -> Tor

You need all three (and finally we have all three, at least to some extent)

A skill file teaches the local model when and how to construct minimally-data-revealing requests to remote models. Use zkAPI-wrapped-with-Tor as a CLI tool.

And everything works! I got the recommendations back, info from frontier models helped to improve them.

Main deficiencies:

* Tor is really not optimized for request-by-request de-linking, which is the only form of network-layer privacy that really makes sense in today's world (long-running identifiers are too fragile). Probably not private enough, and latency 10-100x higher than it could be, at the same time.
* The skill file's request construction strategies are definitely far from optimal.
* Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is still too slow for comfort. It's comfortably running at 20-30 TPS, but it would only really start to feel fast at 100+
* There is a tradeoff: the more careful you are about what data you give to a remote model, the less it can help you

author: lurenbian
quoted_text:
去年 @GCCofCommons 应该通过我们主持的 gitcoin 21 asia round 和单独直接捐赠的方式为 @zkp2p 提供过总计4万美元上下的支持。他们团队本身应该也没有急于商业化，我们也没签任何商业回报条款，后来他们也得到了 @jessepollak 和 @base 的支持和推荐。

昨天注意到 @cbventures @multicoin 投资200万美元的这个 p2p[.]me 背后的产品逻辑和 zkp2p 完全一致。但不同于直接出入金，变成了按单、按消费结算。@ConstantinGao 锐评：“p2p[.]me 更像闲鱼/淘宝中的代付服务”，而现在的代付产业一直是和灰黑产高度绑定的。

大体上应该是用户提交一个付款需求（买咖啡/麦当劳），然后向平台质押相应数额的 USDC。随后p2p[.]me 将付款需求发布在他们的流动性提供商渠道中，最后提供商直接帮用户付法币并凭付款凭证领取用户质押的 USDC。

zkp2p 这种原教旨主义去中心化解决方案大概率要是某个对意识形态和加密朋克价值观本身也感兴趣的团队才会去尝试建设这玩意儿，才会搞出这种 MVP。
但最后 go to market ，真正和黑灰产结合就要看这些老逼登们的了。而这种原生的 p2p 加 zk 证明结合的底层架构即使不成熟不完美但肯定还是能在监管上法律上给灰产大哥们创造更多短期腾挪空间的。

最后该产品的终极形态可能是流动性提供商最后都变成愿意承受 30% 磨损的洗钱者，为用户提供~10% 甚至以上的付款折扣，同时每个消费者本身也可以确保自己不知情，不承担任何额外法律风险。远较传统洗钱生态中的人肉钱骡模式解决方案更优雅。

📊 SoSoValue Macro Daily | Mon, Oct 5
Softer jobs data has eased fears of further Fed tightening. The next test: whether inflation supports that repricing.

What's New

• September payrolls rose 29K vs 90K expected. July and August were revised down by a combined 60K. Private payrolls added 46K, while government employment fell 17K.

• Growth remains resilient. Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% annualized, with consumer spending rising 3.8%.

• August PCE inflation came in at 3.4% YoY, with core at 3.0%. BEA methodology changes, including portfolio management services, complicate the comparison with earlier readings. The lower figures alone do not establish a fresh disinflation trend.

• Energy remains a risk. The G7 announced plans to release 100M barrels of oil and fuel products, with an initial diesel release followed by the remainder over four months.

Our Read
The rally appears to reflect relief over further tightening. Evidence of a sustained inflation slowdown remains incomplete.

Weak hiring adds caution to the policy outlook, while resilient consumption and energy risks keep inflation in focus.

AI investment remains another market driver. Watch whether revenue and returns can justify expanding infrastructure commitments.
